Specialist roles fall off steeply below the top: a top club runs a median of 5 match analysts and 3 sports scientists (32 clubs, 2024); full-time nutritionists work at 14 of 26 Category 1 English academies and at 1 of 63 lower-category academies; and only 14 percent of English non-league clubs have a sports scientist and 4 percent a nutritionist.
items.evidence: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/24733938.2024.2341837 and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35300580/ and https://doi.org/10.3390/app15031050 (research sub-agent, batch 81)

items.text: Performance staff pay falls by division: Premier League fitness and sports-science staff earn about 6,300 pounds more than Championship staff and about 21,800 pounds more than League Two staff (138 staff surveyed, about 2023). Non-player wages across UEFA top-division clubs reached 5.2 billion euros in 2024, with no split by tier.

About three coaches leave with each sacked manager: in one recent English season about 150 coaches lost their jobs alongside about 50 dismissed managers. Some managers bring five or more assistants to a new club, and others hire new staff at each club. No study gives the share of staff who move with a manager, and the season of the English figure needs a check.

No published figures give average staff headcount for English divisions below the Premier League or for the 3. Liga, how common set-piece coaches, loan managers, or data scientists are by division, or non-player wages by tier.

Staff follow a manager in four ways at once: each manager has a trusted inner circle that grows over a career; each staff member decides by personality and by the bond with the manager; the old club can block a move or ask for compensation while a contract runs; and the player's own manager can bring trusted staff to a new club.
items.why: About three coaches leave with each sacked manager, and the movement is personal.

items.text: Staff can be poached: a staff member weighs club size, pay, role, and ambition; a club that takes staff under contract pays compensation; staff can leave for a promotion, for example to a head-coach post; and the player can approach other clubs' staff under the same rules.
items.why: Losing a good coach to a bigger club is part of real football.

items.text: Staff have careers: attributes grow with experience and fall with age; retired players can start as coaches or scouts and carry traits from their playing days; assistants and coaches can become AI managers, so the manager pool grows out of the staff; and staff build a reputation from results and the players they develop, which sets their market value.
items.why: Staff are people, so they need a past and a future as players do.

items.text: What the staff rating shows, and whether each club sees it exactly or through its own judgment.
Each club sees a staff member's rating through its own judgment, so the rating can be wrong, as a scouting report on a player can.
items.why: Staff are seen the same way players are, so no club sees the truth for free.

items.text: Staff carry four more things: knowledge of leagues, regions, and languages that sets where their judgment is sharp; bonds with players, who play better for coaches they trust and may follow them; a workload, so overloaded staff make more errors and a thin department fails in a busy season; and a need for facilities, since staff work better with good training grounds, data tools, and medical equipment that the club business pays for.
items.why: Each of these is part of how real staff succeed or fail.

items.text: Whose judgment sets a club's view of a staff rating: the director of football, the manager's own attributes, or the head of each department.
A contract is negotiated, with a story behind the signature, not filled in as a form.
items.why: A wage and a length typed into a form is the first thing that feels wrong.

items.text: A player weighs more than money when choosing a contract or a club: the role, the manager, the club's project, and life off the pitch.
items.why: A player who counts only the wage is not a person.

items.text: A promise has a cost: when the manager breaks a promise about playing time, a signing, or ambition, the player reacts.
items.why: A free promise is an empty lever.

items.text: The dressing room has structure: leaders, groups, and a pecking order, so unrest can spread and can calm.
items.why: A flat squad cannot carry the mood the board already models.

items.text: A contract carries four groups of parts: money (wage, signing-on fee, loyalty bonus, agent fee), performance bonuses (appearance, goal, clean-sheet, and team success), clauses (release clause, relegation wage cut, promotion rise, option to extend), and promises and status (squad status, playing time, a stated role, and promises about signings or ambition).
items.why: Each part changes a player's choices or a club's money.

items.text: A player's standing in the dressing room comes from four sources: time at the club, ability and fame, a leader's personality, and the captain's armband that the manager gives, where a poor pick loses the squad.
items.why: Real standing comes from all four, and each one gives the manager a different lever.

items.text: Groups form in the squad by language and nation, by age, by starters and bench, and by shared history such as the academy or joining together; a lone new signing can feel shut out.
items.why: Groups are how a grievance or a friendship becomes a squad matter.

items.text: Unrest moves through leaders, who can calm it or spread it; through groups, first inside the player's group and then beyond; into the press, which puts pressure on the manager and the board; and onto the pitch, where a divided squad plays worse together.
items.why: Unrest that stays in one player's mood is not how a real dressing room behaves.

items.text: How much a divided squad plays worse is a design value, because no public match data measures dressing-room division; the value stays below the spread of skill between players.

The manager sees the dressing room three ways at once: some issues show at once, some arrive through people such as the captain and the assistant, and some show only as symptoms whose cause the manager must work out.
items.why: Real managers see the room in part, and each issue reaches them by its own route.

items.text: A divided dressing room has a small effect on the pitch, smaller than the spread of skill between players, so it shows over a season and not in one match.
items.why: The measured skill spread is small, and a larger effect would make the dressing room outweigh football.

items.text: The squad holds a view of the manager, built from results, fairness, and the manager's reputation.
items.why: Respect is what gives the manager's word weight in the room.

items.text: Senior players can go to the board, and a squad that turns on a manager can get the manager sacked.
items.why: Player power is part of how real managers lose their jobs.

items.text: A club has a culture of standards and a winning habit that lasts across seasons; new players take it on or erode it.
items.why: A club is more than the squad of one season.

items.text: A club can have an icon, a player the fans and the board protect, whom the manager cannot easily drop or sell.
items.why: Some players are bigger than the manager at their club.

items.text: A contract runs at most five years, or three for a player under 18, and a protected period of three years (signed before 28) or two years (signed at 28 or older) bans a player who breaks the contract for four months. Squads in the big five leagues average about 2.3 years left on their contracts.

Spanish law requires a release clause in every player contract, and Brazil has a similar system; in England, Germany, and France a release clause is optional. No figures show how common or how large release clauses are elsewhere.

Free transfers are common: 26 to 32 percent of signings in the big five leagues in 2019 and 2020, and 62.5 percent of international transfers in 2025, which carried 0.8 percent of fee value; only 17.7 percent of international transfers had a fee.
items.evidence: https://football-observatory.com/IMG/sites/mr/mr58/en/ and the FIFA Global Transfer Report 2025

items.text: Agent fees are large: clubs paid agents 1.37 billion US dollars on international transfers in 2025, about 10 percent of transfer spending, and Premier League clubs pay about 400 to 460 million pounds a year. FIFA suspended its caps on agent fees at the end of 2023.
A relegation wage cut is reported as usually 25 to 30 percent, within a range of 20 to 50 percent; no count shows how many contracts carry one.

Promises about playing time, squad status, or signings appear to be verbal only, not contract terms; the only written remedy is that an established player who plays in fewer than 10 percent of official matches may end the contract, and rulings on it are rare. Signing-on and loyalty payments are paid in equal yearly instalments in the Premier League.
No published figures give the spread of contract lengths at signing, the share of pay that bonuses make up, how common each clause is, or how often loyalty bonuses and signing-on fees appear.

Four parties shape a contract: the agent, whose skill and greed shape the deal; the director of football, who can negotiate for the club and to whom the player can delegate; the manager, who sells the role and the project; and the family, who can decide a move about country, language, or a child's school.
items.why: A real deal has more than two sides.

items.text: A promise is verbal and moves the player's trust and mood when it is kept or broken, and a few promises can be written as clauses, for example a pay rise after a number of games.
items.why: Real promises are verbal, and only a few terms reach the contract.

items.text: The last year of a contract plays out four ways: some players run the contract down to earn more elsewhere, a player can agree terms with a foreign club six months before the end, clubs sell a player early rather than lose the player for nothing, and personality decides whether a player renews, runs down, or forces a move.
items.why: Free transfers are a quarter to a third of big-five signings, so running down is a normal result.

items.text: Whether an agent is a person with an agenda, a fee only, or a mix where a few powerful agents steer many players; a researcher is measuring how agents shape moves.

The years left on a contract join the shared valuation, as in the CIES fee model, because every club can see them, and a release clause caps the price where one exists. This amends the earlier list of visible inputs to the valuation.
items.why: A player with six months left sells for far less, and free transfers are common.

items.text: A new signing paid more than the established players upsets the pecking order.
items.why: Wages are visible in a real dressing room, and they carry status.

items.text: Bonuses change behaviour: a selfish striker with a goal bonus shoots more often, and a team bonus pulls the squad together.
items.why: A contract term that never reaches the pitch is only accounting.

items.text: The squad status in a contract sets how many matches the player expects, and every missed match counts against it.
items.why: Squad status is the promise most players care about.

items.text: Some players play harder in the last year of a contract, and some coast after signing a long one, as their personality decides.
items.why: Effort that follows the contract is a known pattern in real football.

items.text: Bonus-driven play and contract-year effort are design values small enough that the measured bands still hold, for example the shooting threshold at the edge of the box.

An unhappy player escalates in steps: a private word, a formal transfer request, going public in an interview or a post, poor effort in training and matches that the staff notice first, and in rare cases a refusal to play that costs the player heavily in standing.
items.why: Unrest needs a path to an end, and these are the real steps.

items.text: The manager's discipline tools, such as fines, dropping a player, and training apart, work within the real rules of each country, and going past those rules brings disputes.
items.why: Real football limits discipline, for example a fine of at most two weeks' wages in England.

items.text: Which discipline rules apply in each country, such as the largest fine and the limits on training a player apart.

Few licensed agents earn fees: in 2025 there were 10,525 licensed agents, and only about 15 to 17 percent were paid in an international deal. Deals paying more than one million US dollars were about 12 percent of paid cases and 68 percent of the money.

The agent market is concentrated: in 2010/11 half of big-five players were clients of 83 agents or agencies and a quarter of 24, placed through closed networks with clubs; in 2025 two agencies each represent more than 100 big-five players.

Agents gain from moves more than renewals: the usual dual role is the player plus the buying club (851 of 962 double representations in 2025), and FIFA's rules, largely upheld by the EU Court of Justice in July 2026, cap fees at 10 percent of the transfer fee from the selling club and 3 to 5 percent of wages from the player or buying club.

Agents recruit young players heavily: in 2011, 58 percent of agents' clients were not senior professionals, and FIFA's rules let an agent approach a minor only in the six months before the first professional contract, with a guardian's written consent. No study measures how often players change agents.

Every agent is a person, with a personality, relationships with clubs, and an agenda, but most agents have little power; a few large agencies represent many players and deal often with the same clubs.
items.why: The research shows a concentrated market in which agents gain from moves, and a person with an agenda carries that better than a fee.

items.text: Agents follow the same rule as staff: a full person where an active league needs one, and a light record elsewhere, so ten thousand agents do not slow the save.
Real limits on discipline apply, but a manager with strong standing at the club can push further before a dispute starts.
items.why: It keeps real limits and still rewards a manager the club trusts.

items.text: The manager holds four kinds of discipline tool: a private warning, a fine within the limit, and a suspension for serious cases; dropping a player or sending the player to the reserve team; training apart from the first team; and public pressure through criticism in the press or the transfer list.
items.why: Each tool lands differently on the player and the dressing room.

items.text: When the manager goes past the rules, the player can take a formal dispute to a tribunal and the club can lose and pay compensation, and the board can warn or overrule the manager to protect the club.
items.why: Crossing the line must cost something the manager feels.

items.text: In England the Premier League standard contract caps a fine at two weeks' basic wage for a first offence and four weeks for later offences within twelve months, unless the players' union approves more; a club can suspend a player on full pay for up to 14 days while it investigates, and the player appeals first to the club board and then to the League, with the sanction paused until the appeal ends.

Since 2018 FIFA's transfer rules treat conduct meant to force a player to end or change a contract, such as training alone, as abusive, which gives the player just cause to leave with compensation; under a FIFA and FIFPRO agreement, the rules from 1 January 2027 expressly ban forcing a player to train in isolation or demoting a player as pressure.

Discipline limits differ widely by country: Spain caps a fine at one twentieth of annual pay and bans keeping a player out of training except as a sanction or for injury; Italy caps a fine at 25 percent of monthly pay and allows training apart only as a sanction confirmed by an arbitration board; France bans fines outright and limits separate training groups; Portugal caps a fine at one third of monthly pay per offence; the Netherlands defaults to half a day's wage per week. In Spain, Italy, and Portugal the usual remedy for abuse is ending the contract with compensation.

Every source treats team selection as free: a club may leave a player out of matches without limit, and no rule limits public criticism as such, although dignity and harassment clauses in Italy, Portugal, and France come close. The fine cap for top-division German players is not public.

Discipline follows each country's real rules, yet the real remedy for abuse in FIFA's rules and in Spain, Italy, and Portugal is a free exit with compensation, and the unions take such cases up; the chosen consequences of crossing the line leave out both the free exit and the union. Resolved: the tribunal can award any outcome up to a free exit with compensation, and the union appears only inside the dispute.

A discipline dispute goes to a tribunal that can award any outcome from a warning to a free exit with compensation, following the rules of the club's country, and the players' union appears only inside the dispute.
items.why: It keeps the real remedy without making the union a separate actor in the game.

items.text: Supporters are groups with a history, not an attendance figure and a mood bar.
items.why: A number cannot react to the club.

items.text: Supporters react to what the club stands for: selling the icon, abandoning the style, or raising ticket prices.
items.why: Identity is what fans care about beyond results.

items.text: The press is not a quiz of stock answers: what the manager says has consequences.
items.why: Repeated questions with no effect feel wrong.

items.text: Rumours, leaks, and headlines build over weeks into stories and sagas.
items.why: A single headline with no follow-up does not feel like football.

items.text: The supporter side has four parts: the crowd in the match, whose noise and pressure move home advantage, the referee, and nervous players; fan mood over a season, with expectations, patience, protests, and attendance; groups of fans such as ultras, season-ticket holders, casual fans, and fans abroad, who want different things; and rivalries and derbies that raise the stakes.
items.why: Each part is a way real supporters shape a club.

items.text: The press side has four parts: press conferences before and after matches, whose words reach players, fans, the board, and rivals; journalists as people with sources, slants, and relationships; stories that build, peak, and fade over weeks; and media pressure that moves the manager's job security and the players' mood and form.
items.why: Each part is a way the real press shapes a club.

items.text: The crowd moves three things: the referee, players on both sides whose personality handles pressure badly, and the home team's belief late in a match when it chases a goal.
items.why: The data shows home advantage survives without the referee effect, so the crowd must reach the players too.

items.text: The manager takes part in every press conference and can delegate one to the assistant; where a competition requires players at a conference, the manager chooses which players go; and the manager, staff, and players meet the press in other situations as well. Amended in session 8: under the one delegation model the player may hand over any conference, except where a competition requires the head coach.
items.why: Press work is constant in real football, and choosing who speaks is part of it.

items.text: Stories come from real events in the game and from rumours that journalists invent, and the manager cannot always tell which is which.
items.why: Real transfer gossip mixes truth and invention.

items.text: The crowd's effect on players' nerves and on late belief is a design value that must keep home advantage inside its measured range, because the public data measures the referee effect and the total but not the player effect.
Which competitions require players at press conferences, and which other press duties the manager, staff, and players have; a researcher is finding out.

Supporters hold power four ways: through the board, which protests can move to overrule or sack the manager; through real ownership models such as member clubs with elections, the 50+1 rule, and supporters' trusts; through money, as attendance, season tickets, and shirt sales fall; and through the manager directly, as chants and boos reach the manager's standing and the players' confidence.
items.why: Real supporters hold all four kinds of power, and the kind differs by club and country.

items.text: Each fan group has its own mix of expectations, and the club's fan mood is the balance between the groups.
items.why: Ultras, season-ticket holders, and fans abroad want different things.

items.text: Rivalries come from three sources: known real rivalries in the world data, geography with stronger rivalries in the same city, and events in the save such as cup finals, title races, and a star who moves to the rival.
items.why: A rivalry needs a cause the fans recognise.

items.text: Member ownership joins the owner types of the club business: members elect a president, candidates make promises about signings and the manager, and an election year changes what the board wants.
Known real rivalries arrive only with an imported database, because the game ships no real data; a world with generated names gets its rivalries from geography and events in the save.
How media pressure reaches the manager's job depends on the owner: some owners read the papers, and others listen only to fans or only to results.
items.why: Owners differ, and the owner type already shapes the club business.

items.text: The manager can use the press as well as suffer it: give exclusives that buy goodwill, leak a story on purpose with a risk that it traces back, freeze out a journalist or an outlet with a risk of hostile coverage, and learn over time which journalists are reliable.
items.why: Real managers manage the press, and each tool has a cost.

items.text: UEFA's club competitions require the head coach and at least one player at the press conference the day before a match, 15 minutes of training open to media, flash interviews on matchday (the head coach at least 5 and the player of the match at least 4 if asked), several players through the mixed zone, and the coach at the post-match conference. The FIFA World Cup also requires a player: Senegal were fined 10,000 Swiss francs in 2022 and Argentina 300,000 in 2014 when only the coach attended.

In the leagues checked, the pre-match conference is the manager's: the Premier League names the manager only, and requires weekly player content sessions, a pre-match player interview, super-flash interviews with two players at full time, a half-time interview or dressing-room filming, at least six players through the mixed zone, the manager at the post-match conference, and a pre-season media day. The Bundesliga and Ligue 1 require club conferences without naming who attends; Ligue 1 players pass through the mixed zone but need not answer. LaLiga and Serie A rules are not confirmed.

Words in the media carry real consequences: UEFA fined Ferguson 10,000 euros in 2013 for skipping post-match media, the FA fined Chris Wilder 11,500 pounds for comments about officials, and Ronaldo's 2022 television interview ended his Manchester United contract.

Academies are modelled in full at least down to the under-18 level; below that, the younger players exist as a pool that clubs know only roughly, and over time a club learns which of them are likely to become good or great players; every player of the right age moves up through the age groups.
items.why: A full model of every child is not needed, but the path into the under-18s must be real.

items.text: The youth side has four parts: the academy with its grade, facilities, coaches, and age groups; recruiting young players through scouting, the local catchment area, and taking players from other academies with the compensation that follows; the intake into the professional ranks; and the path to the first team through under-21 and reserve football, B teams, loans, and a debut.
items.why: Each part is a lever a real club pulls on its youth.

items.text: How players move through real academy age groups into professional football; a researcher is finding out.
The world is free to drift over a long save, and the season test bands it, so the quality of the leagues stays inside a real range.
items.why: Real football shifts over decades, and a test is a better guard than a generator that forces the same shape every year.

items.text: New players enter the world by four routes: club academies and their rough pool of younger players; late bloomers found in amateur or semi-professional football; players who rise through the lower leagues; and young players from beyond UEFA who arrive by transfer, held as a rough pool outside the modelled leagues.
items.why: Not every professional comes through a big academy.

items.text: Generated players differ through the style of where they develop, bodies that follow real spreads by position, rare profiles at real rates, and background such as a professional parent or a choice between two nations; more sources of variety may follow the research.
items.why: Players that look alike break a long save.

items.text: Which further real sources of variety make generated players differ, and at what rates; a researcher is finding out.
A young player has no fixed potential number: each player starts with a wide range of possible futures, and the range narrows as the player grows and the five development factors act.
items.why: A fixed ceiling from birth would make development a lottery ticket, and a range keeps the future open.

items.text: A club learns about its young players four ways: through youth scouts and coaches, as good as their own judgment; through time at the club; through physical tests, trials, and strong youth matches; and through other clubs' interest, which is itself a signal.
items.why: Real clubs learn slowly and from several sources.

items.text: Academies run in phases: in England, a Foundation Phase from under-9 to under-11, a Youth Development Phase from under-12 to under-16, and a Professional Development Phase from under-17 to under-23; a scholarship is offered by the under-16 year and a professional contract signed at 17 at the earliest. Every German top-two club must run a graded youth centre, and French clubs use aspirant, stagiaire, and elite contracts from 15 to 20. From 2027, FIFA lets in-house trained under-18s sign contracts of up to five years.

Few academy players make it: about 4 percent of academy players aged 13 to 18 at two LaLiga academies reached the top tier within ten years, and only one in six English players signed at 16 is still in the game at 21. Widely quoted figures such as 0.5 percent of academy entrants turning professional are not primary data.

Academies over-select players born early in the selection year: 45 to 57 percent of academy players are born in the first quarter against about 10 percent in the last, and the LaLiga study found no last-quarter births among the players who made it. Confidence, ball reception, dribbling, and coach ratings separated those who made it.

Moving a young player between academies costs compensation: England's fixed fees rise with age and academy grade, with further payments per first-team appearance and a sell-on share; FIFA's training compensation runs from 10,000 to 90,000 euros a year by club category, and solidarity pays up to 5 percent of a later fee to the clubs that trained the player from 12 to 21. Younger English academy players must live within one hour, or 90 minutes from under-12, unless the academy houses them.

B teams play in the senior pyramid in Spain, the Netherlands, Portugal, and Germany, but must stay below the first team: in Spain at least one division below, in the Netherlands and Portugal with no promotion, and in Germany no higher than the 3. Liga. England uses the under-21 Premier League 2 and invitations to the EFL Trophy instead.

Academies are graded: an English Category 1 academy needs at least 18 full-time staff and a yearly budget of 2.5 million pounds, and German youth centres are graded up to three stars. Barcelona has 44 to 46 academy graduates in the big five leagues, and 30 clubs there have none.

The full player model starts at the scholarship age, about 16, or at the equivalent point in each country's academy system; younger players form the rough pool. This refines the earlier choice of under-18.
items.why: The scholarship is the first real decision a club makes about a young player in every country.

items.text: Clubs over-rate early-born and physically early players and miss late developers, as real academies do, but good youth staff and a manager who knows about the bias can correct it.
items.why: The bias is real and measured, and correcting it is a skill worth rewarding.

items.text: B teams follow each country's real rules: in Spain at least one division below the first team, in the Netherlands and Portugal with no promotion, in Germany no higher than the third tier, and in England an under-21 league and cup invitations instead.
items.why: Real rules keep each country's pathway distinct.

items.text: Squad registration rules belong: homegrown quotas by competition, each country's limits on non-EU players and England's work permits, and squad lists fixed at set dates; a researcher is finding the real rules before the detail is decided.
items.why: These rules make a club's own academy worth more and shape every transfer.

items.text: The player chooses, as with staff hiring, whether to make the yearly decisions on young players (a professional contract, release, or a loan) or to delegate them to the academy head.
items.why: Some players want to shape every youth decision and others do not.

items.text: Brazil, France, and Argentina export the most players (3,020, 2,293, and 2,171 across 135 leagues in 2020 to 2025); per head, Iceland, Montenegro, and Croatia export the most. The foreign share in 31 UEFA top divisions was 42.3 percent in 2022, from 7.9 percent in Ukraine to 74 percent in Cyprus, and only 17 percent of players played at the club that trained them.

Height spreads by about 6 centimetres within a league; goalkeepers average about 190 centimetres and attacking midfielders about 178; leagues differ, from over 184 centimetres in the Bundesliga to about 181 in La Liga; and English top-flight players grew about one centimetre per decade from the 1970s.

Among professionals, birth quarters run 31, 26, 24, and 20 percent, a milder lean than in academies; early-born professionals have no higher transfer values; and in one small Spanish study every player who reached a top-five league was a late maturer, so late developers who make it are a small group with high upside.

About 79 percent of players at the 1998 World Cup were right-footed and very few used both feet equally; about 16 percent of players at the 2022 World Cup were born outside the country they played for, with more than 45 percent in the Moroccan, Tunisian, and Senegalese squads.

No measured rate exists for a professional parent or sibling, for players who play several positions, for very tall or very short outfield players, or for national playing styles; birthplace size has an inconsistent effect, population density a clearer one, and academy players come more often from higher-income families.
Which homegrown, foreign-player, and squad-list rules apply in each country and competition; a researcher is finding out.

The player generator copies four measured patterns: real birth-quarter shares with a small group of late maturers who have high upside, growth of about one centimetre per decade over a long save, each nation's real output of players in total and per head, and eligibility for two nations at real rates.
items.why: Each pattern is measured, and together they keep a long save believable.

items.text: Whether indirect evidence exists for national playing styles, a professional parent, and players who play several positions; a researcher is looking.

International football must fix four things: breaks cost players fatigue, travel, injuries, and mood; call-ups follow a logic the manager can follow and influence; tournaments change players' value, fame, and confidence; and national teams rise and fall, so a player's nation matters to the club.
items.why: Each of these feels wrong when it is missing.

items.text: International football has three parts in the game: the calendar of FIFA windows, summer tournaments, and club release rules; national teams with squads, coaches, rankings, qualifiers, and tournaments simulated as full competitions; and players on duty, with call-ups, caps, travel, fatigue, injuries, and effects on value, fame, and mood.
items.why: These are the parts that reach the club game.

items.text: Managing a national team is a future addition, not part of this programme.
items.why: It is a separate game mode that the club game does not need first.

items.text: Registration rules differ by competition: UEFA's club competitions allow 25 players on List A with 8 places for locally trained players (at least 4 club-trained, meaning three seasons between 15 and 21), plus an unlimited List B for young players; the Premier League allows 25 plus under-21s with at least 8 home-grown; Serie A 25 plus under-22s with 8 trained in Italy; the Bundesliga requires 8 locally trained players and 12 Germans with no non-EU limit; LaLiga allows 3 non-EU players and ties registration to a squad cost limit; Ligue 1 allows 4 non-EU players.

England's work permits since 2021 follow a points system with up to four exception places for top-two-division clubs; foreign-player limits change over time and by country, for example Turkey moved between 5, 8, 11, and no matchday limit between 2014 and 2025, Russia rose from 8 to 13 registered foreigners in 2022, and the Netherlands sets a minimum salary for non-EU players instead of a quota.

About 55 percent of outfield players in the top five leagues play one position group and just under 30 percent play two, measured from real appearances; rating data suggests most midfielders are versatile, centre-backs and strikers much less so, and versatility peaks at ages 24 to 26.
items.evidence: https://www.statsandsnakeoil.com/2020/08/10/finding-the-most-versatile-player/ and the FIFA 22 player ratings (people's ratings, not measurements)

items.text: Evidence for national playing styles is weak: league styles are measured (the Premier League most direct, the Bundesliga the most counter-attacks), but they describe leagues, not nationality; rating databases show small differences by nationality of 1 to 6 points, which may reflect raters' stereotypes and which players move abroad.
items.evidence: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333330546 and https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1080/17461391.2010.481334 and the FIFA 22 player ratings

items.text: No base rate exists for a professional parent or sibling: elite athletes are more than 2.3 times as likely as others to have a father who played competitive sport, and famous sons make up roughly 1 percent of World Cup 2026 squads, a lower bound.
A player's style comes from where the player develops, the league and the academy, and not from nationality. This replaces national styles in the list of sources of variety.
items.why: League styles are measured, and the nationality differences in rating data may be stereotypes.

items.text: Whether versatility copies the measured split of about 55 percent in one position group and 30 percent in two, and which design rate sets a professional parent, at about 1 to 3 percent.

A call-up follows four signals: club form and minutes weighted by league level, the national coach's own style and favourites, loyalty to established internationals, and the depth of the nation, so a player from a small nation is called up at a lower level.
items.why: The manager can follow a call-up that rests on signals like these.

items.text: The manager and the player shape international duty four ways: minutes at the club raise the chance of a call-up, the manager can ask the national coach to rest a tired player and the coach may refuse, a player eligible for two nations chooses one and the manager or the family can sway the choice, and an older player can retire from international football.
items.why: Each is a real lever around international duty.

items.text: International duty changes four things: fatigue from matches and travel, with long-haul trips costing more; injuries on duty, with compensation to the club; mood and confidence from a first cap, a good tournament, or being left out; and value and fame from a strong or poor tournament.
items.why: Breaks and tournaments must cost and reward something.

items.text: FIFA's calendar has international windows in September, October, November, March, and June; clubs must release players for them; and FIFA pays clubs for World Cup players and compensates clubs for injuries on duty. This is the agent's recall, not yet checked.
The manager gives team talks before the match, at half time, and at full time, and the words move the players' mood and focus.
items.why: Team talks are one of the manager's most direct levers, and no session had named them.

items.text: Clubs can fall into crisis: takeovers, owners who run out of money, administration, and points deductions.
items.why: Real clubs collapse and change hands, and a long save needs that risk.

items.text: The manager's week is part of the game: how reports, messages, and decisions reach the manager, the calendar of training, travel, and press, and limits on the manager's time.
items.why: Every new system this session sends something to the manager, so the flow of information needs its own design.

items.text: The realism test reaches the world off the pitch: it bands the measured off-pitch facts, such as sackings, manager tenure, the share of free transfers, and agent fees, and gives every design value a design target that a test checks, such as transfer requests per season.
items.why: A growing part of the game rests on design values, and a design value with no target is never checked.

items.text: Delegation works the same way everywhere: every decision area can be delegated, and the player sets how much to hand over. This joins the separate delegation choices for staff hiring, set-piece design, contract talks, press conferences, and youth decisions into one model.
items.why: Five separate delegation rules would confuse the player.

items.text: Over a long save the rules of football change, as they do in real life, for example FIFA's 2027 transfer rules, foreign-player limits, and competition formats. You did not choose this when it was offered.

The manager's week must fix four problems: an inbox flooded with noise, time that costs nothing, days with no rhythm of match day, recovery, training, and travel, and events whose reasons stay hidden.
items.why: Each makes the week feel unreal.

items.text: A team talk feels real when the right words depend on the score, the mood, and each player's personality; when repeating one approach loses force and a rare outburst lands harder; when the manager can speak to single players; and when a respected manager gets more from the same words.
items.why: A talk that is the same pick every time is a routine, not a lever.

items.text: Information reaches the manager through a daily inbox that the player can filter, weekly or monthly reports from delegated work, and urgent issues that staff escalate at once.
items.why: It keeps the inbox familiar while cutting the flood at the source.

items.text: The reasons behind events are visible in a mixed way, as in the dressing room: some causes show at once, some come through staff, and some the manager must work out.
items.why: The same rule across the game lets the manager learn without being told everything.

items.text: Time is spent as a few weekly focus choices, such as leading one training session, a scouting trip, or a meeting with a player, while staff cover the rest; long trips block days. A budget of hours would feel like bookkeeping.
How the manager's time is limited in the way that makes the game most enjoyable.

Only 18 of the 36 schema attributes reach a match calculation. The other 18 (crossing, heading, long shots, technique, anticipation, work rate, concentration, teamwork, strength, agility, balance, jumping, handling, aerial reach, throwing, command of area, communication, rushing out) feed only the AI manager's role-fit score, or nothing.

Attribute effects are linear on a 1-to-100 scale: for example, top speed is a base plus a fixed amount times pace divided by 100, so the step from 90 to 100 is worth the same as the step from 50 to 60.
The engine already keeps a player's base values apart from the effective values play reads, but fatigue is the only thing that lowers the effective values today.

A role today is a set of attribute weights that the AI manager uses to pick a player for a slot, and a duty is only a depth offset and a risk offset. Neither changes how a player behaves with or without the ball.
The six team instructions already map to numbers the engine reads, for example pressing sets how many players press and how far they go.
Every attribute has a named job in at least one engine calculation, and an attribute with no job is removed or given one.
The effect of an attribute is non-linear at the extremes, so the step from 90 to 100 matters more than the step from 50 to 60 and elite players stand out.
Consistency, big-match temperament, injury proneness, and professionalism are hidden attributes that scouting reveals in part.
Condition, match sharpness, morale, form, and minor knocks modify effective ability in one layer, and never change the base attributes.
Every tactical setting (line height, pressing intensity and triggers, width, tempo, directness, and mentality) maps to a number the engine reads.
A role and duty become behaviour weights, for example an inverted full-back moves into midfield in possession and a target forward holds up play and draws long balls.
A sensitivity test raises one attribute on one player over a large batch of matches, and passes when the related statistics move in proportion and unrelated statistics do not move.
No single attribute, usually pace, dominates, and no two attributes measure the same thing.
The data-model area opens with attribute jobs: every attribute gets a named job or is removed, and overlaps and pace dominance are settled there.
items.why: Half the attributes do nothing in a match today, which is the widest gap.

items.text: The sensitivity test is a test family of its own beside the realism test, and it runs at every milestone: one attribute raised on one player over a large batch, related statistics moving in proportion, unrelated ones still.
items.why: The realism test bands whole-match outputs only, so a dead attribute passes it.
items.accepted-risk: One batch per attribute, 36 or more batches at every milestone, makes each milestone run slow.

items.text: Every one of the 36 attributes keeps its place and gets a named job in the engine; none is cut or merged.
items.why: You want the full genre list, and each attribute must earn its place.
items.accepted-risk: Teamwork, work rate, and communication act on the team, so they need team-level mechanisms that do not exist yet.

items.text: Attributes intermingle in their effects: a calculation reads several attributes together, not one attribute per calculation.
items.why: Football actions draw on several qualities at once, and a blend stops any single attribute carrying an outcome alone.

items.text: Pace is kept from dominating three ways together: it acts mainly in long runs while acceleration decides short races, every sprint costs stamina so a fast player who runs often fades late, and the sensitivity test fails pace when its effect is out of proportion.
items.why: Real top speed is rare, 0.7 percent of live time above 7 metres per second.

items.text: All four overlaps are settled while the jobs are written: vision, decisions, and anticipation; composure and the pressure trait; technique and first touch; agility and balance; plus at least one pair you have not named yet.

The blend mixes three rules: an action runs in stages (see, choose, execute, under pressure), each stage has one main attribute with two or three smaller supporting weights, and the weights are fitted from real data where it exists and set by design where it does not.
items.why: Stages give each mental attribute its own moment, a main attribute keeps the rule readable on screen, and fitted weights keep it honest.
items.accepted-risk: Several stages per action add calculations on every tick, which presses on the engine's CPU tripwire that the other realism additions already strain.

items.text: Vision sets which passing options a player can see; decisions sets how well the player picks among them and when to act; anticipation sets how early the player reads an opponent's next action, for interceptions, runs, and loose balls.
Four more pairs are settled with the jobs: pace and acceleration; heading, jumping, and strength; aggression and tackling; concentration and consistency.

The overlap splits hold with your changes. Pace is top speed in long runs; acceleration decides short races and how fast a player reaches top speed. Jumping is height and timing; heading is what the player does with the ball on contact; strength holds position in contact and also acts well beyond the aerial duel. Aggression is how often and how hard a player commits, with the foul risk, and it also acts beyond the tackle; tackling is success once committed. Concentration acts through the whole match, and its weight rises as the match goes on; consistency is the spread of a player's actions within a match as well as between matches. Technique shapes how every action is done and which skills a player can attempt; first touch is control on receipt. Agility is speed of turning and also gates hard actions such as overhead kicks, diving headers, and certain tackles; balance is staying up in contact and striking off balance. Composure acts on each action under pressure; the pressure trait acts on big occasions.
Concentration now acts through the whole match and consistency now spreads actions within a match too, so both move a player's errors inside one match.

Technique and agility both decide which hard skills a player can attempt, so an overhead kick or a diving header could read either attribute, and technique risks becoming a general 'better at everything' number.
After attribute jobs, the data-model area goes to the scale and elite players.

Concentration is rare sudden lapses, such as a loose back pass or a lost runner, more likely as the match goes on; consistency is the everyday spread of each action around the player's level, within a match and between matches.
items.accepted-risk: Lapses are rare, so the sensitivity test needs larger batches to see a change in concentration, which adds to the slow milestone runs.

items.text: Hard skills are gated three ways together: each skill has a technique threshold and an agility threshold; ball skills such as flicks, volleys, and chips lean on technique while body skills such as overhead kicks, diving headers, and slide tackles lean on agility; and technique decides whether the player tries the skill while agility decides whether the body pulls it off.
Attributes use a 1-to-20 scale everywhere: the engine stores what the manager sees.
items.why: It is the genre's familiar scale, and the screen never hides finer steps.
items.accepted-risk: Whole steps are coarse, so development and the per-attribute age curves move a player in visible jumps of one point, and a small gain waits until it adds up to a whole step.

items.text: The curve that makes the top of the scale matter more acts in both places: on each attribute before the blend, and on the blended result of each stage.

Which curve maps a rating to an effect, whether 1 to 100 was too wide, what spread of ratings the world should hold across all attributes, and how real football reasons about the spread of player ability; a researcher is looking.

Football Manager shows attributes on 1 to 20 and keeps a hidden current ability on 1 to 200. An attribute point costs more of that ability budget above about 17, so top points are scarce because they are expensive, not because the display is curved.

Football Manager is reported to move attributes in hidden fractions behind the whole-number display. A young player gains at most about one visible point per attribute per season, and two to three visible points across all attributes; the best tested season was about 11 ability points at age 21 against about 1 at age 28.

Across 18,207 FIFA 19 players the overall rating is close to normal (mean 66.2, spread 6.9): 3 percent sit at 80 or above, 0.6 percent at 85 or above, and 14 players at 90 or above. Single attributes spread wider and lean left because of specialists. Market value grows about 1.21 times per rating point.

Club Elo puts the English tiers at about 1839, 1608, 1491, and 1387, so the largest drop is from the first tier to the second (about a 79 percent win expectancy) and the drops shrink further down; elite clubs sit near 2030 to 2046.
The world holds about 128,700 professional male players at about 3,990 clubs.

No published study shows that underlying skill is heavy-tailed. The honest reading is that skill is close to normal, while what depends on it (value, wages, goals) is convex and right-skewed, as superstar economics predicts; player value models show a thin elite over a dense middle.

A contest decided by the gap between two ratings on a logistic curve, as chess Elo does, gives 20 against 18 the same odds as 12 against 10. To make the top gap matter more on the pitch, each rating must first pass a convex map, for example an exponential, before the gap is taken. Baseball's 20-to-80 scouting scale sets 10 points to one standard deviation and stops at three.

Storing attributes as whole numbers from 1 to 20 pulls against development: at one or two visible points a season, a player would sit still for whole seasons and age in jumps, which is why Football Manager is reported to keep hidden fractions.
The engine stores attributes in tenths from 1.0 to 20.0, and the screen shows whole numbers from 1 to 20.
items.why: Development and ageing move smoothly, while the screen keeps the genre's familiar scale.
items.accepted-risk: Two players shown as 15 can differ slightly in play.

items.text: Each rating passes a convex map before a contest takes the gap, set so the gap from 18 to 20 counts about twice as much as the gap from 10 to 12.
items.why: A gap on a logistic curve alone treats every gap the same; the double weight is close to how Football Manager prices its top points.
items.accepted-risk: One elite player can carry a weak team in some matches.

items.text: A player's overall level follows a normal curve centred on 10 with a spread of about 3.5 on the 1-to-20 scale, wider than the research suggestion of 2.8; single attributes spread wider still, each tier has its own mean, and the largest drop is from the first tier to the second.
items.why: Tiers overlap more, so a lower-league gem is common.
items.accepted-risk: The world shows more upsets than real football, which presses on the cup upset band and the per-match realism bands.

items.text: The convex payoff lives in three places: on the pitch through the curve before the gap, in development where top points cost more to gain, and in the market where value and wages grow about 1.45 times per point.
items.accepted-risk: Three curves to tune, and their effects compound.

items.text: The factor of two for the top gap was picked, not measured, so the strength of the convex curve needs a target it is set against.

The strength of the convex curve is set against the five-match target: a top player looks clearly better than an average player in the same role in about two of three runs of five matches. The factor of two for the top gap is only a starting value.
items.why: The factor of two was picked, not measured, and the five-match target is already the board's measure of felt quality.
items.accepted-risk: The target sets the whole curve, not the top gap alone, so the top gap can end at any ratio the target allows.

items.text: One effective-ability layer holds four families of temporary state: body states (in-match energy, carried fitness, match sharpness, minor knocks), mind states (morale, confidence, form), familiarity (position rating, tactic familiarity, partnerships), and surroundings (crowd, pitch, weather).
Each state acts on its own attributes: tiredness hits the physical attributes first, low morale the mental ones, a knock the physical ones, and sharpness the timing of technical actions.
The layer can raise a player as far above the base attributes as it can lower the player below them.
items.accepted-risk: The attributes on screen tell the manager less about what a player does today, and the base quality that the five-match target measures is blurred by a larger swing of temporary state.

items.text: Match sharpness is its own state that rises with minutes and falls without them, and it also feeds carried fitness and form.

The layer's total swing is limited but meaningful even when all four families act at once: an 18 never suddenly becomes a poor player, but poor patches and hot streaks do happen, and a hot player never becomes unstoppable. Body states and mind states carry the largest shares of the swing.
items.why: A strong player must stay strong, while temporary state must still be felt.

items.text: Match sharpness is its own state that rises with minutes in matches and falls without them, and it also feeds carried fitness and form.
Each family of temporary state has its own cap on how far it moves a player, and the caps add; body and mind have the largest caps and surroundings the smallest.
The size of each family's cap on the 1-to-20 scale, set so that all four together never make an 18 a poor player and never make a hot player unstoppable.

Consistency and injury proneness are hidden values, beside the twelve hidden personality traits; injury proneness replaces the visible injury-resistance attribute. Amended in session 8: the twelve traits are now thirteen personality attributes.
items.accepted-risk: The manager learns them only by watching and through staff, over seasons.

items.text: For the manager's own players, the visible attributes are exact once the player signs; hidden values stay hidden.
items.accepted-risk: Scouting matters only for the market, and a signing shows its true visible numbers on the first day.

items.text: A hidden value shows itself to the manager in words, for example 'thrives on big occasions', with a confidence set by the staff, as personality already does.

Every role ships with all three behaviours together: where the player stands in and out of possession, which actions the player prefers, and how teammates treat the player (a target forward draws long balls).
items.accepted-risk: It is the largest piece of work and the most tuning in the data-model area.

items.text: A duty (defend, support, attack) scales the role's own behaviour, for example an attacking full-back overlaps more and tracks back less.
items.accepted-risk: Every role needs three tuned variants.

items.text: The game offers the full genre list of about 40 roles.
items.accepted-risk: With three duties and three behaviours each, about 360 tuned variants, and many roles differ only slightly.

items.text: The sensitivity test also changes one tactical setting or one role over a large batch and checks that the expected statistics move, for example a high line gives more offsides against.
items.accepted-risk: More batches at every milestone, on top of the batch per attribute.

items.text: About 40 roles, many of them close to each other, pull against a sensitivity test that fails any role whose change moves nothing measurable: several close roles may fail, or pass only because the test tolerance is loose.
The sensitivity test compares each role with a neutral default, not with its nearest neighbour, so close roles pass as long as each one does something.
items.accepted-risk: Two roles can be near-duplicates in play while both pass.

items.text: The data rules of the player (a job for every field, one scale, and a sensitivity check) are examined for four more kinds of data: team-level numbers, the other rated people, relationships and history, and the physical and fixed facts.
Of the wider data, team-level numbers come first: cohesion, club style, tactic familiarity, and team mood.
items.why: They feed every match.

items.text: Each kind of wider data gets its own data rules, decided as the kind is examined, rather than the player's rules applied unchanged.
items.accepted-risk: Slower, and the kinds may drift apart in scale and in how they are checked.

items.text: Team numbers today have three problems: nothing shows what they change, familiarity and partnerships may be counted twice (in each player and again for the team), and club identity is a word rather than a number the engine reads.
Team numbers act on actions that need several players at once: pressing chains, the offside line, and combinations between pairs.
items.why: A team can be more than its players, for example in coordinated pressing.
items.accepted-risk: A second place to tune beside the player layer.

items.text: Team numbers acting on team actions pull against the familiarity family of the player's effective-ability layer, which already carries partnerships and tactic familiarity, so the same thing may count twice.

The player layer keeps what is personal, the position rating and the player's grasp of the tactic; partnerships and cohesion move to the team layer and act only on actions that need two or more players.
items.why: Each quality then counts once.

items.text: Club identity acts only off the pitch; it reaches play only through what the club does off it.
Team numbers join the sensitivity test: raising cohesion or one partnership over a large batch must move only team actions, for example pressing chains regaining the ball more often.

Identity acting only off the pitch pulls against the earlier decision that a club's style has three layers, identity, squad, and tactic, each adding its own part to how the club plays, and against the assumption that the engine keeps identity as a separate style input.
How club identity is created and how it evolves.

On the pitch a club's style comes from two layers, the squad and the tactic. Club identity shapes both from outside by two routes: it shapes who the club hires and buys, and the board and fans expect it, so a manager who plays against it loses standing and the AI manager weighs it in its philosophy.
items.accepted-risk: Two slow loops to tune, and style on the pitch no longer carries a separate identity input for the realism test to check.

items.text: A club's identity at the start of a save is seeded from the real club's history and reputation, with a fallback where no source exists.
items.accepted-risk: It needs a data source for the clubs of every active league.

items.text: Identity drifts slowly towards how the club actually plays when it wins, and jumps at big events such as a takeover, a legendary manager, relegation, or a trophy.
items.accepted-risk: The most tuning of the three ways identity can change.

items.text: What happens when a manager wins with a tactic against the club's identity.
Which source seeds identity where no real history exists.

When a manager wins against the club's identity, three reactions mix, and each club sets their strength: results buy time, supporter groups split between results and style, and at clubs with a strong identity a winning manager can still lose standing over time.
items.accepted-risk: At some clubs a manager can be sacked while winning, which some players of the genre find unfair.

items.text: Where no real history exists, identity is computed from the simulated past seasons the save generates: how the club played and won.
Height sets a player's standing reach in the air, jumping adds to it, and heading decides what happens on contact; tall players also turn a little slower, so height is a trade-off.
items.accepted-risk: Agility and height both touch turning, so the sensitivity test must separate them.

items.text: Build is a description such as slight, athletic, or powerful, generated from the attributes, with no effect in the engine; weight is not stored.
items.accepted-risk: Build is a field with no engine job, the kind your brief warns against, although it is shown as a word and derived from attributes that do have jobs.

items.text: Besides the age curves, age acts directly: older players recover more slowly between matches, carry more injury risk under congestion, and fade faster late in a match.
items.accepted-risk: Age overlaps stamina, natural fitness, and injury proneness, so the sensitivity test must separate them.

items.text: A player new to a country adapts over months: language, climate, and the league's style move the mind family of effective ability, beside the off-pitch effects of nationality.
items.accepted-risk: One more state to track for each player.

items.text: A relationship between two people carries two numbers: on-pitch understanding, earned from minutes together, and personal liking, moved by personality, groups, and events; two players can combine well and dislike each other.
The game stores every pair at every club in the active leagues, and none at the light clubs.
items.accepted-risk: Memory and save size grow with the number of active leagues, on top of the full staff and agent records already chosen for them.

items.text: Each player keeps every event of recent matches, for replays and deep reports, and match summaries for older ones.
items.accepted-risk: Large saves, which adds to the load on the player's machine that session six already named as the sharpest risk.

items.text: Both numbers of a relationship fade when two people are apart, at different speeds.
Every rating in the game, for staff, managers, referees, and agents as well as players, uses the 1-to-20 scale stored in tenths.
items.why: One scale to learn.
items.accepted-risk: The referee's numbers are sized from published data in the engine's own units, so each must be converted to and from the 1-to-20 scale.

items.text: Every staff, manager, and agent rating has a named job, and a season-long sensitivity check runs before each release.
items.accepted-risk: Season-long batches are slow, on top of the match batches at every milestone.

items.text: The referee's numbers are hidden: the manager sees a description such as 'strict with cards' before the match and learns more from past matches.

A shot today is a physical kick: the shooter aims at a spot whose width grows with finishing, noise shrinks with finishing, and the goal comes from the ball's flight and the keeper's reach. The keeper holds a fast ball with one flat chance of 86 percent, with no keeper attribute in it.
The engine computes an xG for each shot from distance and angle alone, and uses it only for the match report; it never decides an outcome.

A tackle today is a small chance on each tick for each opponent within reach, 5 percent times tackling divided by tackling plus dribbling. It reads no acceleration, agility, positioning, anticipation, or angle of approach.
Every action has a success probability built from the situation and the attributes, followed by a random draw.

Shot outcomes follow an xG model from distance, angle, body part, shot type, defensive pressure, and the shooter's and keeper's abilities: penalties about 75 to 80 percent, most shots from outside the box under 5 percent, and about 10 percent overall.
Pass success reflects difficulty: distance, pressure on the passer, defenders in the lane, the receiver's movement, and the pass type, modified by technique and vision.
A duel compares the relevant attributes in context: acceleration, agility, and dribbling against tackling, positioning, and anticipation, with the angle and speed of approach.
Errors come from conditions: pressure, fatigue, low composure, and poor decisions cause misplaced passes, poor touches, and keeper mistakes, which give realistic goals from errors.
Variance is calibrated to real football: stronger teams win more often, while draws and upsets happen at realistic rates.
Simulated shot conversion, grouped into xG buckets, matches the expected probability of each bucket.
Across a season team strength correlates strongly with points, while single matches still give believable upsets.
The xG-bucket check judges the engine with an xG model fitted on public real shots, reading distance, angle, body part, shot type, and pressure, independent of the engine.
items.why: The engine must not mark its own homework.
items.accepted-risk: The event contract and the test-only output must carry body part, shot type, and pressure for every shot.

items.text: The resolution model sits between pure physics and pure probability: physics with a measure of probability.

A probability is drawn at each contact, the moment a player touches the ball or the ball meets a player: the tackle, the first touch, the keeper's handling, and the quality of a strike or a pass. Each draw comes from a chance or a spread built from the situation and the attributes. Between contacts, flight, deflections, bodies in the lane, and the keeper's position are physics.
items.why: Real data measures outcomes at contacts, so they calibrate directly, and physics between them keeps blocks and interceptions emergent; the xG buckets then check the whole chain.
items.accepted-risk: Two systems to tune, and a bad xG bucket can come from either one.

items.text: The strike's draw mixes a named strike quality (a clean strike, a scuff, a slice) with an error in aim, height, and power from a spread built from finishing, technique, composure, pressure, body part, and the weaker foot.

The keeper's contact mixes physics (position and dive decide whether the ball is reachable) with a draw (reach, hold, or parry from the shot's speed and placement and the keeper's own attributes), and keepers need attributes of their own for it.

A penalty mixes a guessing game with an ordinary strike: the taker picks a side, the keeper guesses with habits the other side can learn, and the strike's error and the keeper's reach then apply as for any shot.
Three checks guard against shots that are too accurate: the xG-bucket check, a band on the split of wide, blocked, and on-target shots, and conversion by distance.

A keeper's save mixes physics and draws: the keeper's position and dive decide whether the ball can be reached; only then a draw decides hold, parry, or fumble from the shot's speed and closeness and the keeper's handling, with composure under pressure; a small third draw sets a parry's direction, weighted away from goal by a good keeper. One-on-ones set how the keeper narrows the angle; rushing out and command of area act on crosses and through balls.
Keepers also carry every outfield attribute, and every outfield player carries hidden goalkeeper attributes, generally poor, set at creation and never developed.
items.why: An outfield player who must go in goal, or a keeper who plays with the feet, reads real values.

items.text: A strike takes two draws: first a quality (clean, scuff, slice), which pressure or a bad touch can force, then the error in aim, height, and power inside that quality, from finishing, technique, composure, pressure, body part, and the weaker foot.
items.accepted-risk: Two draws per shot to calibrate, and more work on each tick with a shot.

items.text: Keeper behaviour works from the outfield attributes wherever they fit: the dive reads agility and the keeper's stance reads positioning, with no separate diving or keeper-positioning attribute.
items.accepted-risk: An agile outfield player in goal dives like a keeper, limited only by the hidden poor keeper attributes.

items.text: A pass is a contact whose draw adds an error to direction, weight, and height, from passing and technique, the pass type, pressure on the passer, the weaker foot, and body shape; vision and decisions act earlier, in the choice. When a defender in the lane can reach the ball, a draw from anticipation and positioning decides whether the defender cuts it out. The receiver's run sets where the ball is met, and receiving is its own first-touch draw from first touch, ball speed and height, and pressure at receiving.
The pass model is checked by completion by pass kind, by length, and by pressure at receiving, and by how often players choose the safe open receiver compared with real players.

Every outfield attribute can act for a keeper: tackling joins rushing out and one-on-ones when a keeper goes to ground at a forward's feet, eccentric keepers sometimes dribble, keepers can score, and keepers have flair.
Keepers carry an eccentricity, a hidden tendency that sets how often a keeper dribbles, comes far out, or tries the unusual.

A duel runs in two steps: physics decides the approach, the angle and closing speed from pace, acceleration, and positions; a first draw decides whether the defender commits or holds off, from decisions and aggression; then the contest draw reads the attacker's dribbling, agility, acceleration, balance, and strength against the defender's tackling, positioning, anticipation, and aggression, with the angle, the closing speed, and the local numbers.
items.accepted-risk: Two draws per duel, and duels are the most common contest in a match.

items.text: A duel ends in one of four outcomes: the attacker keeps the ball, the defender wins it clean, the ball runs loose, or a foul.
items.why: When a defender wins, possession changes only about half the time, so loose balls are a real phase.

items.text: The duel model is checked by win rate by local numbers, the foul share of duels (about 11 percent), dribble success by third, and the turnover split after each winner.

Errors come from three sources: the far tails of every contact draw, whose spread widens with pressure, fatigue, low composure, and low consistency; rare concentration lapses that grow late in a match; and a small set of named error events (a short back pass, a keeper spilling a cross, a slip), each with its own chance, so commentary and reports can name them.
items.accepted-risk: Three sources to calibrate; each takes a fixed share of the band.

items.text: The measured rate of goals that follow an error, by data provider, and which definition to band against; a researcher is looking.

Opta counts an error as one on-the-ball mistake, or a keeper's spill or failed claim, that directly leads to a shot or a goal. In the Premier League, errors led to 91, 119, and 167 goals in 2022-23 to 2024-25: about 0.24 to 0.44 a match, or 8 to 15 percent of all goals. Teams range from 1 to 18 a season, and keepers make about a quarter of them, about 0.1 a match.
All error events, leading to a shot or a goal, run at about 0.6 to 0.9 a match in both Opta and StatsBomb data, and roughly 35 to 45 percent of them end in a goal.

High turnovers, possessions that start within 40 metres of the opponent's goal, run at 11 to 17 a match in the Premier League, 15 to 17 percent end in a shot, and they give 0.2 to 0.33 goals a match; many are won by pressing rather than given away.

The realism test bands errors on Opta's definition, with a wide band: errors leading to goals at 0.25 to 0.45 a match (8 to 15 percent of goals), keepers about a quarter of them, and a team spread that depends on quality and composure. It adds a check on high turnovers: 11 to 17 a match, 15 to 17 percent ending in a shot.
items.why: It is the public, per-team measure fans see, and the season-to-season swing is large.
items.accepted-risk: High turnovers mix pressing wins with errors, so a failure there may point at the pressing model rather than at errors.

items.text: The season variance bands (the home, draw, and away split, the share of points spread explained by quality, top-quarter against bottom-half results, and Poisson goals) each carry the real target and a design target with a little more upset; the test passes on the design target and reports the distance from real football.
items.why: The wide world spread of ability was chosen on purpose and gives more upsets than real football.

items.text: Team strength is measured two ways for the season check: a strength from the ratings of each club's best eleven must predict points, and an Elo-style rating built from the simulated results must match real Elo spreads between clubs and tiers.
All four costs would hurt a player: waiting on matchdays, save creation time, save size, and memory.
The game promises to run well on an ordinary laptop, about 4 cores and 8 GB of memory.
items.why: The widest audience.
items.accepted-risk: Tight limits on matchday time, save creation, save size, and memory, against a world of full people, every pair, and full recent events.

items.text: The budget has two forms: fixed limits for what the player feels (matchday wait, save creation time, save size, memory) on the reference laptop, and a relative limit per match against the shipped engine as an early warning in the tests.

A budget on an ordinary laptop pulls against the rich world chosen this session: every staff member and agent as a person, every pair stored, every event of recent matches kept, and more draws on every tick.

No realism lever is pulled to meet the budget: background matches keep the full engine, the active leagues stay as the player chooses, people and pairs stay full records, and every match keeps its events. Amended in session 8: one named exception, the analytical-models work group, whose cheap stand-in runs outside the watched match.
items.accepted-risk: On an ordinary laptop the budget is very likely to fail, since today's engine already takes about 20 seconds per league season on eight cores and this session multiplied the work per tick and the data per save.

items.text: When the budget fails, engineering gives way first: the team optimises (parallel matches, compact storage, cheaper maths) until the budget holds, and returns to you only if it still fails; no realism is cut before then.
items.accepted-risk: An open-ended amount of optimisation work.

items.text: The fixed limits on the reference laptop: the longest matchday wait, the longest save creation, the largest save, the most memory, and the relative limit per match against the shipped engine.

The repository already has a calibration run: 1000 matches per sample over 17 bands, among them goals per match 2.4 to 3.2, goalless share 4 to 12 percent, shots on target share, corners, yellow cards, sending-off share, pass accuracy 75 to 88 percent, and goals per xG. The bands are still the wide first guesses, not the measured ones the board chose.
The calibration report compares two arms of one run (a feature flag off and on); it keeps no history across engine versions, and no automated job reruns it after each change.

Per-match targets for both teams together: about 2.6 to 2.9 goals, 24 to 26 shots, 8 to 9 on target, 9 to 11 corners, 20 to 24 fouls, 3.5 to 4.5 yellow cards, a red card in about one match in eight to ten, and pass completion about 78 to 85 percent.
Goals spread roughly as Poisson, with 0-0 in about 7 to 8 percent of matches and occasional high-scoring games.
Champions finish on about 80 to 100 points in a 38-match season, relegated clubs on about 20 to 35, with a sensible spread between.
Each division is calibrated separately: lower leagues have lower pass completion, more direct play, and different goal rates.
An automated harness runs thousands of matches, writes a statistical report, reruns after every engine change, and stores each report for comparison with later versions.
Of the calibration gaps, per-division calibration comes first.
Which recent multi-season figures, per league and per division, with each provider's definitions, set the per-match targets; a researcher is looking.
A division's style emerges from its players and their tactics, with nothing set per division by hand; the bands check the result per division.
Every league in the world gets its own set of bands.
items.accepted-risk: Most leagues have no public match data, so most of their bands are guesses or copies of a similar league, and a failing guessed band may send tuning the wrong way.

items.text: Where a league has no public match data, its bands come from a formula fitted on the leagues with data, by tier and by league strength.
items.accepted-risk: The formula extrapolates beyond its data, so a league unlike any measured one can get a wrong band.

items.text: The season check bands the league table in full, per league, with real and design targets: champion points, the points of the relegated places, the spread of points per game, and the title margin; both the full engine and the fast model must pass.

Each engine change runs a quick set of a few thousand matches automatically, and a full run of many thousands runs before each release. Every report is stored with its version and compared with the last one, and a band that moves by more than its tolerance is flagged even when it still passes.
items.accepted-risk: A few thousand matches on every change costs minutes of machine time per change, and the repository has no automated job to run it yet.

items.text: Each band's tolerance is the real spread of the statistic across leagues and seasons, widened by the sampling noise of the batch size, so a small quick run does not fail by chance while a full run is judged tightly.
The distribution check compares the share of every scoreline (0-0, 1-0, 1-1, up to 4-3 and beyond) with real shares, and compares the goals, shots, and cards totals as whole distributions.

Across 2021-22 to 2025-26 the top five leagues average, per match for both teams: 2.83 goals, 25.2 shots including blocked shots, 8.8 on target, 23.8 fouls, 9.7 corners, 4.08 yellow cards, a red card in 16.8 percent of matches, 0-0 in 6.3 percent, a 43.6, 25.3, and 31.1 percent home, draw, and away split, and 82.0 percent pass completion on Opta's count. Leagues differ: LaLiga shows reds in 22 percent of matches, the Premier League in 11.

Lower divisions pass less and play more directly, clearly in England: pass completion falls from 82.2 to 78.0, 72.2, and 69.3 percent down four tiers, passes per team from about 452 to 370, and the long-ball share rises from 4.7 to 7.4 percent. Continental second tiers pass only 2 to 4 points worse but draw more (26 to 32 percent) and see more 0-0s (up to about 10 percent).

In 2021-22 to 2025-26 top-flight champions took about 2.3 points per game (84 to 95 points in 38 matches in England, Spain, and Italy), 18th place about 0.9, and the spread of points per game across a league was about 0.46; second and third tiers are flatter, at about 0.33.
