The decision that accumulated load raises injury risk pulls against the evidence that the acute-to-chronic workload ratio does not predict injuries and creates artefacts.

Training shapes fitness at three scales: each day's session adds load and moves fitness, and a good plan follows a match-day rhythm of recovery, load, and taper; a preseason builds a fitness base that the off-season loses, so a short preseason means a weaker base and more early-season injuries; and the fitness staff design the plan by their quality when the manager delegates, and warn when the manager's plan overloads the squad.
Illness such as colds, flu, and stomach bugs happens at real rates by season and can spread through a squad, with a few days out and reduced output on return.
items.accepted-risk: A spreading illness can strip a squad before a key match, which a player may find unfair unless the staff's warnings and prevention make it manageable.

items.text: The medical staff decide routine care. For serious injuries the manager chooses among the options the staff present, such as surgery or rest, a specialist, or a second opinion, each with its time out, cost, and recurrence risk; the player and the agent also have a say, so a player may seek his own specialist or refuse surgery. Better staff and facilities shorten returns and cut recurrence.

An injury reaches the mind three ways: a return after a long injury lowers confidence for a while, by personality, and a good start restores it; the player is cautious in the actions that caused the injury, such as fewer committed tackles after an ankle injury, fading with minutes; and the long-term injured feel isolated and frustrated, which staff, the manager's contact, and team-mates can ease.

Elite players fall ill about once every second season, with a median of 3 days out (58 percent respiratory, 38 percent stomach), peaking in winter; respiratory infections in the Bundesliga cost about 12 days each. No football data measures spread within a squad, so spread is a design choice.

A full stop in the off-season costs 3 to 21 percent of aerobic capacity, against 1 to 4 percent for players who stay active, and two weeks off takes two to three weeks to rebuild. Teams average 30 preseason sessions (10 to 51); each 10 more go with 22 fewer days lost per 1000 hours in season and one point more match availability, a weak but real link. Training injuries spike in July.

An irregular match schedule, not total volume, goes with severe muscle injury across 30,097 player-seasons in the top five leagues, and load spikes carry 5 to 7 times the injury rate; compensatory training keeps non-starters' fitness tests level but leaves them exposed to a spike when they play.

Jet lag lasts about a day per time zone, worse eastward, and stayed raised four days after an 11-zone trip; away disadvantage grows with time zones crossed, but regular travel did not raise injuries. At about 43 degrees high-intensity running fell 26 percent while pass success rose; cooler northern clubs had more injuries and warmer southern clubs more ACL injuries; altitude favours the higher team.

Treatment choices change time out: a partial meniscus removal returns in about 4 months against 6 for a repair, and a high ankle sprain 71 days after surgery against 39 without; surgery on some hamstring tears gives similar returns with fewer re-injuries. Days lost per injury type differ widely between clubs, lower where medical and performance staff communicate well and higher after head-staff turnover.

Fear of re-injury is common after a hamstring injury and goes with both re-injury and lower performance; after a severe hamstring injury, top speed and high-speed running took up to five weeks of matches to recover, and a mild quadriceps injury about a week.

High-intensity running differs by role: wide midfielders about 3,140 metres a match, central midfielders 2,830, full-backs 2,610, attackers 2,340, centre-backs 1,830. Extra time runs about 10 percent below regulation for high-intensity running, speed, and distance, with accelerations and technique falling most.

Every match builds sharpness by its level, first-team matches most, then cups, reserve and under-21 matches, then friendlies, and training slows the loss. A match-simulation training session builds some sharpness at a load and injury cost, so a manager can keep a bench sharp without matches. Irregular minutes carry their own risk: a player thrown in after weeks without matches faces a load spike.

Travel adds to accumulated load by distance; crossing time zones adds a jet-lag state of about a day per zone, worse eastward, that dulls decisions and slows recovery; climate moves in-match drain and injury risk, with heat cutting high-intensity running and cold raising muscle risk; and the club plans travel, such as flying one or two days before by charter or scheduled flight, trading cost against recovery.

Fatigue differs by role and time: each role's movement sets its own drain, so full-backs, wide players, and pressing forwards tire faster; a substitute enters with full reserves after a short warm-up curve; extra time continues the reserves about 10 percent below regulation output and adds clearly to the next days' load; and players recover a little during in-match breaks, such as half-time, the breaks before and within extra time, and long stoppages.

Every player everywhere carries condition, load, sharpness, and injuries. The fast model draws injuries and minutes from the full engine's distributions, and AI managers in background leagues rotate by the same rules, so the market, form, and scouting see real availability.

A pre-transfer medical by the buying club's medical staff reads injury proneness and site history at their accuracy, and the club can walk away, renegotiate the fee, or add injury clauses. The shared market valuation also falls with visible injury history, such as days missed in recent seasons, so injury-prone players are cheaper for everyone.

An injury crisis reaches beyond the pitch: the board asks why, and the medical and fitness staff's standing falls when burden runs above what their quality should give; overplayed players lose morale and complain, while a squad that sees the manager protect players trusts him more; and the press runs injury-crisis stories, with fans blaming the manager or the medical staff.

The season injury and fatigue bands are judged on full-engine seasons in the release run, and the fast model is checked against those seasons' distributions; between releases, the engine emulator screens injury and fatigue settings so the release run only confirms.
A save keeps daily load and state for recent weeks, a longer window for players in the active leagues, and a compact injury record (type, site, date, days out) for every player's whole career.
items.accepted-risk: Per-player state for every player everywhere adds to save size beside every pair and full recent events.

items.text: Match performance feeds form, morale, player development, reputation, and market value, and minutes and the quality of performances drive growth in young players.
Results move board confidence, fan satisfaction, finances, and the manager's job security.
Feedback loops are dampened, so winning teams do not become unstoppable and struggling teams can recover.
No match feels meaningless within the season.
Multi-season simulations show a realistic turnover of champions and a realistic variation in team fortunes.

Titles concentrate: in 2000 to 2010 the Premier League had 3 champions and the Bundesliga 5, while in 2010 to 2020 the Bundesliga had 2 (Bayern won 11 in a row) and Serie A 2 (Juventus won 9 in a row); Lyon won 7 in a row, Rosenborg 13, and Scotland has two clubs. Champions' share of available points in the big five rose from 69.9 percent (1999 to 2004) to 80.5 percent (2014 to 2019), and imbalance rose across 24 leagues.

Points per game is the team statistic that predicts next season's points worst; goal difference and expected-goal difference predict better. The table after about 12 rounds correlates about 0.8 with the final table, and the leader on 1 January won the title in 9 of 20 seasons. No clean football figure exists for the season-to-season points correlation; the NBA shows 0.64 and the NFL 0.33.

Since 1995, 47 percent of clubs promoted to the Premier League went straight back down and 60 percent within two years; all three promoted clubs fell in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Of 42 relegated clubs from 2009-10 to 2022-23, 40.5 percent returned within a year, 64.3 percent within two, and 31 percent never; parachute clubs were almost twice as likely to go up.

Wage bills explain 80 to 90 percent of league position, and wages predict better than net transfer spend. Studies find competitive balance fell after UEFA's Financial Fair Play, because a cap tied to revenue locks in hierarchies built on past success; parachute payments soften the drop but skew the second tier.

Football results show no hot hand: after controlling for strength, a win streak is followed by slightly worse results, and repeating the last result is slightly less likely than chance. Sacking a manager in a slump mostly rides regression to the mean; Dutch clubs that kept the manager recovered faster.

Playing in Europe costs little in the league: Europa League clubs did better domestically than matched non-qualifiers over 16 seasons, and a Champions League midweek costs about 0.1 points in the next league match, while European clubs make about 94 starting changes a season against 71.

Minutes are a leading predictor of market value for players first seen under 21, but no public study sizes how much minutes at 18 to 21 raise later ability; under 30 percent of loanees are 21 or younger, and players who stay at their training club have better careers.

Football Manager long saves drift: generated players shift in attributes over decades, big AI clubs leave high-potential youngsters without minutes, and AI clubs stop buying the stars they need; league reputation moves about one point a year, which damps drift but makes it sticky.

A young player's growth has three layers: training sets the base rate by coaches, facilities, and personality; minutes at the right level of challenge add the most, fastest when the match level sits a little above the player's ability; and good performances add a small extra. Growth moves within the player's narrowing range of futures.

Form runs at two speeds with a fading memory, so no match drops out suddenly: a short form of about three matches feeds mood and selection, and a long form of about a season feeds reputation and value.

After each match the board reads four things, weighted by owner type: points against what the squad's strength and budget predicted; the trend, so a run of bad results counts more than one loss and a recovery softens it; big matches, such as derbies, finals, and rivals; and style and academy minutes against the owner's targets.

A player's reputation moves four ways: ratings and minutes weighted by the level of the league and competition; big stages, such as finals, European nights, and tournaments, which count more; a bias toward visible goals and assists, as real scouts and media show, so creators and defenders are undervalued and good scouting finds an edge; and a slow fade without minutes or at a lower level.
Form feeding mood, and mood moving decisions, can make a winning streak breed more wins, while real results show no hot hand and a slight reversal after win streaks.

Mood stays without a runaway streak three ways: mood effects stay small and a season check bands streaks against real data, so a win streak is no more likely than chance; after a run of wins some players, by personality, relax and cut effort, while after losses some fight harder; and opponents raise effort and set up more cautiously against a leader or a team on a run.

Four forces limit a rich, winning club: each league's real rules, such as revenue sharing, parachute payments, spending rules, and salary caps where they exist; wage pressure, as success raises contract demands and rival offers; ageing and poaching, as squads age together and bigger clubs buy the stars and the manager; and rivals who react, as AI clubs spend and change tactics to catch the leader and rival owners invest after failures.

Balance comes first from real mechanisms, plus a gentle hidden pull toward the middle inside AI club decisions, such as transfer and wage choices, that the multi-season check tunes to a pooled real band.
items.accepted-risk: A hidden pull can feel like rubber-banding if players discover it, so the pull must act only through AI choices a real club could make and never on match outcomes.

items.text: A struggling club recovers four ways: it sells stars, cuts wages, and buys cheap young talent that grows; new owners take over at real rates, sometimes with bad results; luck evens out, and the game shows the manager the underlying numbers, such as expected goals, so an unlucky slump reads as unlucky; and a strong academy now and then produces a golden generation that lifts the club for some seasons.

Every match keeps its weight four ways: the game shows the stakes before it, such as projected places, qualification and relegation chances, board and fan pressure, and prize money per place; mid-table clubs chase secondary goals, such as a cup run, a top-half finish, academy minutes, a record, or a rival's result; matches with nothing at stake change players, as some switch off, some play for a contract or a place, and the manager can try players and tactics; and press, rivalry, and records give each match a story.

Results move income four ways: real prize money per league place and cup round; attendance and season tickets that follow fan mood with a lag, so a bad season costs money the next season; commercial deals that renew at values set by reputation and recent success; and large European sums, which is one of the loops that entrenches the top and one of the loops the multi-season check watches.

A manager's job security builds and falls over seasons: trophies, promotions, and seasons above expected build credit that fades slowly; success raises the board's targets, so an over-performance becomes the next target; a new owner resets credit, targets, and patience; and AI clubs sack at real rates and moments, such as long losing runs, the relegation zone, and season end.
A player's market value mostly follows long form and reputation over seasons, but a big tournament or a breakout half-season moves it quickly, as real hype does.

The multi-season check bands three families: title turnover (distinct champions per decade, the longest title run, and how often a champion retains the title); fortune churn (season-to-season rank correlation, how often a top-four club drops out, and how far clubs rise and fall over ten seasons); and up and down rates (promoted clubs' survival, relegated clubs' return within one and two years, and yo-yo clubs). The champion's points share is not banded.

The multi-season check runs ten saves of fifty seasons each, so slow drift, such as generated-player attributes, reputation, and wages, shows as well as turnover; background leagues use the fast model.
items.accepted-risk: Ten saves give few title-turnover samples per league, and fifty full seasons of the active leagues may not fit the overnight release run on the Mac mini and the VPS, so the size needs a cost check.

items.text: The multi-season check bands against one pool of real history across leagues, because a save's history diverges from real history anyway; the soft pull in AI choices is tuned to that pooled band.

Four guards stop long-save drift: each year's generated youth cohort is anchored to a fixed target distribution by country and position; AI clubs give young players minutes by a real share and loan them when they cannot; AI clubs plan squads, replacing ageing stars and filling gaps each window; and club and league reputations drift toward a long-run value set by money and results, so no club stays big or small by inertia.
Match preparation must avoid four faults of the genre: it must not become a weekly chore, its effect must be visible, it must not become an exploit, and both sides prepare.
items.why: The person named all four as true of management games today.

items.text: Preparation has four parts: knowing the opponent (report, likely line-up, injuries, habits), the match plan (selection, tactic, opposition targets, set-piece plan), the training week (rehearsal against the opponent, drilling routines, rest), and the briefing (the team meeting and each player's job).
Preparation helps only where the squad can carry out the plan: a plan beyond the players does nothing.
items.why: It ties preparation to the squad fit that already emerges from play, instead of a free bonus.

items.text: Preparation costs staff workload and training time: analysts and coaches have limited capacity, and opponent work displaces fitness, development, and routine sessions, so even a rich club gives something up.
No public study measures the effect of opponent-specific preparation on its own; real home advantage, about 0.3 goals per match, is the nearest scale.
items.evidence: general knowledge of the home-advantage literature; no preparation study known

items.text: Four parts of preparation before every match pull against the decision that preparation must not become a weekly chore.

Knowing the opponent carries the area: the report and the analysts' read are the part the game builds best and shows most, and the plan, the training week, and the briefing follow from what the staff find.
When the week gets heavy, the training week is handed over first: the coaches set the sessions from the manager's plan.
items.accepted-risk: The balance of rest and rehearsal is the coaches' choice, not the manager's.

items.text: Every week the staff prepare every part by default, and the manager changes only what the manager wants, as delegation works in every other area.
items.why: It stops preparation from becoming a weekly chore without cutting any of the four parts.

items.text: A better analyst's report predicts the line-up and shape more often, finds more of the opponent's habits, says honestly how sure it is, and arrives earlier. Separate analyst attributes drive the line-up, the habits, and the confidence; the timing comes only from how busy the analysts are, which ties it to the workload cost.
items.why: Every rating keeps a named job, and timing through workload makes the cost of preparation visible.

items.text: Surprises that beat a good report come from four sources: real change (injuries, suspensions, rotation, a new manager), the opponent's hidden adaptability, strong managers who hide their plan on purpose, and leaks both ways through the press and players.
items.accepted-risk: The manager's own press conferences and unhappy players can leak the manager's plan, and the report is least reliable in the biggest matches.

items.text: The post-match report lists each prepared point and whether it worked, traced to its moments through the true-cause log.
AI managers prepare against the manager by reading the manager's whole fingerprint over seasons, as the manager's analysts read theirs.
items.accepted-risk: An established style becomes predictable, so a long-serving manager faces opponents who know the manager's habits.

items.text: Preparation has no cap on its effect: only squad fit limits it, and the exploit hunt catches the rest.
items.accepted-risk: No band can fail when preparation grows too strong, so an exploit that the hunt misses reaches players.

items.text: Preparation with no cap and no band pulls against the in-game management decision that every tool's effect is banded on forked matches with paired seeds.
Preparation has no cap in the mechanism, but the forked-match check measures its effect on paired seeds and flags any value outside a wide design band set after playtests.
items.why: It keeps preparation inside the rule that every tool's effect is banded, without fixing a number no study supports.

items.text: Rehearsal against one opponent gives each player a short-lived grasp of this match's specific instructions, which fades after the match, on top of the lasting grasp of the tactic.
items.accepted-risk: One more short-lived value per player for each match.

items.text: The briefing acts three ways: it raises how faithfully each player follows the opposition targets, it adds what each player knows about his direct opponent to his picture of the pitch, and it moves mood and focus as part of the pre-match team talk.
Analysts need more than three attributes: like every staff role, they carry a properly decided set of attributes, personality types, and hidden attributes, each with a named job.
items.why: The person raised it when asked for the top risk of match preparation: three attributes under-specify a role the area leans on.

items.text: A staff member's attributes have three layers: a small core every staff member shares, a role set designed from the real job, and specialism tags such as good with young players, so the trade-offs sit in the tags.

Staff personality uses the players' twelve traits plus a few staff-only traits, such as loyalty to a manager, ambition for the top job, and honesty in advice, so a retired player keeps his personality when he becomes a coach.
Of the staff hidden values, consistency carries the most weight: how much a staff member's work varies week to week, as the hidden consistency of players does.
The full attribute lists for each role are decided after research into what real clubs assess for each role, then role by role in the brainstorm.

A club's view of a staff member's ratings comes from the judgment of whoever makes the hire: the manager's own attributes when the manager hires directly, and the head of the department when the hiring is delegated.

Staff grow three ways: work at a club a little above their level grows the attributes fastest; courses and licences the club pays for grow them further, at a cost in time away and fees; and licences are required for some roles and competitions, as real rules demand.

UEFA coaching licences take about 60 hours (C), 120 (B), 180 (A), and 360 (Pro, over at least one season); the Goalkeeper A and Elite Youth A take 120 hours each; holders revalidate with at least 15 hours of training every three years. In 2017 Spain had 2,379 Pro holders, Germany 861, and England 383.

Coaching research splits a coach's knowledge into professional (the sport), interpersonal (people), and intrapersonal (learning from one's own practice), and UEFA's Pro licence has a matching professional-coach area beside the player and team, the training environment, and the match.
In a survey of 125 Dutch scouts, scouts felt unable to judge a prospect's potential before age 14 to 15, and they judge by a mix of structured criteria and gut feel.
Ten of the twenty Premier League clubs had a dedicated set-piece coach before 2025-26, and Chelsea paid about 750,000 pounds in compensation for one.

A survey of all 78 top-flight clubs in four leagues found about 11.0 medical and performance staff per club in England, Spain, and Italy against 6.9 in Germany, with 3.6 against 1.8 physiotherapists and 1.8 against 0.5 strength and conditioning coaches.

In UEFA's elite club injury study, clubs with poor communication between the doctor and the manager had 82 percent match availability against 88 percent and 76 percent training attendance against 83 percent; each grade better of communication between medical and performance staff meant about 4.1 fewer days lost to hamstring injury per 1,000 hours.

In the same study, a change of fitness coach or team doctor went with significantly more hamstring injury, and a new head coach who brought his own fitness staff went with about three times the hamstring burden in that season.

No study measures the week-to-week consistency of football staff work; the nearest evidence is decision fatigue, where clinicians make worse choices as a session wears on, and in hospitals each extra patient per nurse raised mortality by about 7 percent.

Athletes value honesty, trust, confidentiality, and approachability in practitioners, and club doctors and physiotherapists who report to coaches lose players' trust, which lowers what players disclose.
An English Category 1 academy must employ at least 18 full-time staff on a budget of at least 2.5 million pounds a year.

Every staff member carries a shared core of five attributes: football knowledge sets the base accuracy of all advice; communication sets how much of a report or instruction is taken up; man management sets how fast bonds with players form; reflective learning sets how fast the person grows over a career; and work rate sets how much workload the person carries before errors rise.
items.why: Coaching research splits a coach's knowledge into professional, interpersonal, and intrapersonal kinds, and real data ties communication to player availability.

items.text: Staff carry five staff-only traits beside the players' thirteen: loyalty to a manager, ambition for the top job, honesty in advice, discretion (whether the person leaks), and openness to new methods.

Staff carry five hidden values: consistency, which weighs most and worsens under workload; rapport, whether players tell this person about a knock or a problem; awareness of blind spots, whether the person warns when advice falls outside the specialism; adaptability to a new club's style; and tolerance of long hours, the workload ceiling.

Three pairs overlap and break the rule that every overlapping pair has one split: work rate and tolerance of long hours both set workload; the hidden adaptability to a club style and the players' adaptability trait share one name; and man management and rapport both act on how players relate to staff.

Staff carry three hidden values: consistency, which weighs most and worsens under workload; awareness of blind spots, whether the person warns when advice falls outside the specialism; and tolerance of long hours, how fast the person burns out over a season of overload.
Work rate sets a staff member's capacity in a week, and tolerance of long hours sets how fast the person burns out over a season of overload.

A staff member has no separate value for adapting to a new club's style: the person's playing idea and openness to new methods decide how fast a style clash fades, and adaptability keeps one meaning, the trait for settling in a new country and culture.
Rapport is not stored: whether a player tells a staff member about a knock or a problem comes from the bond between that player and that staff member, and man management sets how fast bonds form.

The director of football carries six role attributes: squad planning (a view three to five years ahead that flags expiring contracts and gaps), negotiation (fees and wages in talks), financial acumen (budgets and spending rules), coach appraisal (how well the director judges managers and staff, which sets the view of delegated hires), network (early word on available players and loans), and data fluency (the ability to use analytics, split from openness to new methods, which is the willingness).

The head of recruitment carries five role attributes: profile fit (matching targets to the club style), scout management (how many assignments run at once and how well reports combine), succession planning (a plan per position, split from the director, who plans the whole squad), agent and club relations (the odds that a first approach succeeds), and combined judgement (how much noise the head removes when several scouts report).

A scout carries six role attributes: judging current ability, judging potential, and judging character (each sets the noise of one estimate), report structure (criteria against gut feel, which sets bias against random error), birth-date and maturation correction (whether early-born and early-maturing youths are over-rated), and data use (accuracy when scouting by video); the tags carry only regional knowledge and biases.

The loan manager carries four role attributes: judging a loan club's environment (predicts growth and minutes), loan-club relations (whether minutes and role clauses are honoured), player welfare (the remote care of players away from the club, split from man management of the squad), and loan monitoring (the accuracy of progress reports).

The assistant manager's candidate attributes are in-match reading (the quality of suggested substitutions and changes), staff coordination (spreads workload and cuts delays), man management, and tactical knowledge (accuracy of pre-match advice); the trim to one cohesive set removes the overlaps with the core.

A first-team coach's candidate attributes are session design (how fast the squad learns a tactic), teaching style (how fast individual attributes grow), content rated separately for attacking, defending, technical, and tactical work (which training areas improve), and tactical breadth (how many tactics or phases the squad can hold).

The goalkeeping coach's candidate attributes are keeper technique, keeper distribution, keeper profiling, and mental preparation; the set-piece coach's are routine design, routine capacity (how many routines the squad holds), defending set pieces, and reading opposition set pieces.

The fitness coach's candidate attributes are conditioning (late-match fade) and load management (training fatigue against gains); youth coaches carry development coaching (youth growth rate) and learning environment (youth morale and drop-out); the academy manager carries pathway management, curriculum consistency (one club style across the age groups), and talent identification (quality of the youth intake).

Every staff member carries one shared list of attributes; each role reads a weighted part of that list, and a staff member's suitability for any role is computed from the list, as a player's rating per position is. The role walk collects candidates, and a trim merges the overlaps into the list. The core, the traits, the hidden values, and the tags stay.
items.why: Staff move roles and have a suitability beyond their current role.

items.text: The match and opposition analyst's candidates are tactical understanding (finds opponent habits), line-up prediction (a design choice), calibration (how honest the stated confidence is), communication, workload management (report timing), and data interpretation.

The set-piece analyst reads the analyst attributes for dead balls; the data scientist's candidates are modelling (less noise in model-based player ratings), uncertainty (error bars on those ratings), data coverage (which leagues have usable data), and translation (explaining to staff who are not technical).

The club doctor's candidates are pitchside emergency care (accuracy and speed of head-knock advice), diagnosis (how far the shown layoff differs from the true one, and the chance a knock is missed), illness control (how fast illness spreads, a design value), and medical ethics (whether players disclose to this doctor); the head of medical's are department leadership (lowers errors below them), communication with the manager, and communication across departments.

The physiotherapist's candidates are assessment (shows accumulated load, catches hidden knocks, fitness tests, medicals), treatment (shorter layoffs, less recurrence), rehabilitation planning (pacing through return phases), and injury prevention (lower hazard through screening); the rehabilitation coach's are on-field reintegration (sharpness on return, fewer relapses) and progression judgement (speed against recurrence risk between phases).

The sports scientist's candidates are load monitoring, data interpretation (quality of rest and rotation advice), recovery protocols (condition recovery, jet lag and climate plans), and persuading the coaches (whether the manager accepts the advice); the strength and conditioning coach's are programming (raises the sprint and slow reserves, lowers landing and turning hazard), lifting technique (training-injury rate), and physical profiling (shows fitness ceilings).

The nutritionist's candidates are fuelling and recovery, body composition (slows physical decline), and travel nutrition; the sport psychologist's are performance psychology (confidence and pressure handling), wellbeing and referral (catches low morale or a crisis), profiling (shows hidden traits of signing targets), and confidentiality (whether players open up). Their effects are design values, because no study sizes them.

The head groundsman's candidates are turf science, recovery under use, weather management, and surface consistency; the team manager's are travel planning, handling disruption, and rules administration; player care's are relocation support, welfare radar, and transition support.
There is no separate translator: every staff member has a languages list, player care reads it and carries cultural bridging (climate and league-style settling, loneliness).
The specialism tags go through the same trim as the attributes, and a tag survives only where it carries a trade-off no attribute can.
Staff change carries no separate rule: a new fitness coach or doctor starts with no bonds and no knowledge of the players, and the injury cost of the change emerges from that.
Weak evidence from a review chapter says abnormal playing surfaces raise lower-limb injury about 2.6 times, and the same review says natural-turf hardness is not proven to cause injury.

The shared staff list holds 47 attributes. Core: football knowledge, communication, man management, reflective learning, work rate. Coaching: session design, teaching, attacking, defending, technical, and tactical coaching, tactical breadth, goalkeeping coaching, set-piece design, set-piece coaching. Judgement and analysis: judging ability, judging potential, judging character, judging staff, calibration, data analysis, modelling, tactical analysis, line-up prediction, in-match reading. Management: squad planning, negotiation, financial acumen, network, department leadership, player pathway, logistics, rules administration. Medical and performance: emergency care, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, prevention, physical assessment, conditioning, load management, recovery, sport psychology. Care: welfare, settling support. Grounds: turf management, weather management. Medical ethics and confidentiality merge into the honesty and discretion traits.

Ten specialism tags remain, each a leaning or a trade-off no attribute carries: youth developer, veteran whisperer, early-maturer bias, motivator, disciplinarian, aggressive return to play, conservative return to play, soft-tissue specialist, concussion-cautious, and club-first doctor.
Managers use the shared staff list: a manager is a staff member whose role reads a weighted part of it, so an assistant's suitability to become a manager is computed like any role.

The shared staff list holds 32 attributes. Core (5): football knowledge, communication, man management (players and staff), reflective learning, work rate. Coaching (6): tactical coaching (how fast and how much tactic the squad holds), attacking, defending, technical, and goalkeeping coaching (each sets how fast that area grows), and set-piece coaching. Judgement and analysis (7): judging ability, judging potential, judging people (character and staff), calibration, data analysis, opposition analysis (line-up and habits), in-match reading. Management (5): squad planning (including the player pathway), negotiation, financial acumen, network, administration (logistics and rules). Medical and performance (7): diagnosis (including pitchside care), rehabilitation (including treatment), injury prevention (including load management), physical assessment, conditioning, recovery, sport psychology. Care (1): player care (welfare and settling). Grounds (1): groundsmanship (turf and weather).
items.why: Merges join attributes that drive the same mechanism or that one role always reads together.
items.accepted-risk: Four risks at once: a season-long sensitivity check for each of the 32 attributes adds to the check load; full staff records add to save size and memory; about 25 roles need weights over 32 attributes, all design values; and only communication and staff continuity have measured effect sizes.

items.text: A better analyst's report predicts the line-up and shape more often, finds more of the opponent's habits, says honestly how sure it is, and arrives earlier: opposition analysis sets the line-up and the habits, calibration sets the confidence, and timing comes only from how busy the analysts are.

The human manager's tactical attribute acts on information accuracy, how fast the squad learns a new tactic, and how the squad's mood and trust respond to the manager's choices, but managers now read the shared staff list, which has no single tactical attribute.

The game must answer four faults of deep management games: overwhelm at the start, losing without knowing why, a game that is easy once solved, and a new player punished with a sacking before learning the game.
items.why: The person named all four as true.

items.text: The game serves genre veterans and football fans new to the genre: a new save asks how much the player knows and sets the defaults to match.
items.accepted-risk: Two first-hour paths to design and test.

items.text: Difficulty comes from two levers: the club the player chooses, as in Football Manager, and a setting for how much help and explanation the player gets. Neither moves the match engine, the results, or the AI.

Every area can be handed to staff; for a player who said at the start that the genre is new, areas open over the first season, each introduced by the staff member who runs it, while a veteran starts with everything open; and for everyone the assistant points each week to what matters.

The help setting moves how much the game explains (plain summaries, why a figure matters, what to look at) and how often it pauses to point at a key moment; it never changes how accurate staff readings are.
items.why: Staff readings stay wrong in proportion to staff quality, so the staff market keeps its value.

items.text: A sacked manager keeps the career and looks for a new job, as real managers do, and the save continues.
AI clubs copy what wins across the world, as real football copies trends, so a winning idea stops being new; this widens the set-piece drift the board already allows to tactics.
items.accepted-risk: The world's style drifts over a long save, so the season test must keep league styles inside real ranges while trends move.

items.text: The manager's time is limited by the structure of the week, as in Football Manager: a fixed number of training session slots, one team briefing per match, and similar fixed moments. There is no budget of hours and no burnout of the manager.
items.why: The person wants the limits of the real week's structure, not bookkeeping.

items.text: When the manager does a task personally instead of handing it to staff, the task uses the manager's own attributes from the shared list, better or worse than the staff member's, and bonds with the players and staff involved form faster.

The week's fixed slots are: training sessions per day and week, which match days, travel, and recovery days reduce; one briefing per match and one team talk before, at half-time, and after each match; the press conferences each competition requires; a limited number of one-to-one meetings per week, a weekly staff meeting, and trips that block days. Some inbox messages need a reply by a deadline, and a message left unanswered goes to the staff default or lapses.

One-to-one talks are limited three ways: the manager has a few routine talks per week and the assistant handles the rest by default; talking to the same player again soon loses effect and can annoy him; and talks that an event opens, such as a request, a dip in form, or a contract issue, do not use a weekly slot.

The manager's three effects map onto the shared staff list: information accuracy reads opposition analysis and judging ability, the squad's learning speed for a new tactic reads tactical coaching, and the squad's mood and trust response reads man management; the AI manager's in-match choices also read in-match reading and opposition analysis.
A manager's action blends the manager's attributes with the attributes of the staff involved, so a manager's information comes from the analysts' work read through the manager's own attributes.

The viewer today draws a flat top-down 2D pitch on one canvas, plays at 1, 2, 4, or 8 times speed with its own pause, shows a goal banner timed in real time so it stays readable at 8 times, and warns when the stream cannot keep up.

Watching the match must answer eight faults: play that is hard to read, matches too long or too short, unreal movement, no way to look back, repetitive commentary, figures cut off from play, no sense of occasion, and no control of the view.
items.why: The person named all eight as true.

items.text: The base view is the top-down pitch with height: the ball's shadow, a lift for players in the air, and a slight tilt for depth. Players stay circles for now, and a tilted pitch with figures may come later.
The player can pause and rewind through the match so far, then return to live, and after the final whistle can replay any part of the match, linked from the report.
Other matches show live scores and key events during the player's match, and their highlights are available after the final whistle; the player does not switch to watch them live.

The sense of occasion comes from three things, built in this order: crowd sound that rises with danger and the size of the match, with commentary on top; a pre-match build-up with the stakes, the story, the line-ups, and the weather; and a pitch that shows the ground's size, weather, wear, and a crowd edge that fills with attendance.

The player controls the view two ways: overlays toggled on the live view (shape lines, pass and run arrows, player state such as tiredness, and heat zones), and zoom with follow of the ball or one chosen player.

Football Manager 24 offers five highlight modes (Key, Extended, Comprehensive, Full Match, Commentary Only), changeable during a match, with separate speed sliders for play and for highlights; FM26 adds a dynamic mode that shows more highlights as a tense match nears full time and fewer in a one-sided one, and fills the time between highlights with a 2D overview and data cards that link to clips.

Football Manager players complain that Extended highlights take about 20 minutes with 2 to 3 minutes of dead time before a highlight, that the FM26 engine looks arcade-like with scorelines that are too high, and some watch whole matches in 2D because it shows movement and positions most clearly. No source confirms a rewind, a post-match full replay, custom highlight rules, or control over how much build-up a highlight shows.
items.evidence: SI bug tracker r41240 (search snippet); https://www.altchar.com/reviews/football-manager-2026-review-a-disappointing-step-backwards-a6QHj3y0USb4 ; Steam FM19 discussion

items.text: FM26 offers seven cameras (2D Classic, Behind Goal, Aerial, Broadcast, Tactical, Dynamic Sideline, Vertical Scrolling) with adjustable height and zoom, an in-match xG graph and momentum widget, assistant advice that uses xG, automatic goal replays with angles by goal type, and a pause on injury.

Match length is set four ways: a five-mode ladder (key moments, extended, comprehensive, full match, and commentary only) fed by the board's highlight ranking and changeable during a match; a dynamic mode that shows more as the match grows tense; every shown moment starting early enough to show its build-up; and custom rules the player sets, such as all set pieces or only the own team's attacks.
items.why: Rewind, custom rules, and build-up control would set the game apart; no source shows them in Football Manager.
items.accepted-risk: Four viewing features to design, tune, and test.

items.text: Between highlights the pitch keeps playing at high speed, so the player sees the shape of play without detail.
The realism test also bands movement: player speeds, turn rates, and accelerations against real tracking data, so a slide or a snap fails a check.

The briefing acts on all three: each player's picture of his direct opponent, how faithfully players follow the opposition targets, and mood and focus. This amends the rule that no instruction lands weaker because of the manager, for opposition targets through the briefing.
items.why: Session 7 already let faithfulness to choice instructions vary with the player's decisions and teamwork.

items.text: Work rate and tolerance of long hours apply to AI managers and to staff who become managers, never to the human manager, whose time is limited only by the structure of the week.
Managers carry a hidden value named tactical flexibility that sets how often a manager breaks habit; adaptability keeps its one meaning, settling in a new country.
A delegated hire is judged by the department head, and the director's coach appraisal corrects part of that error when the club has a director.

AI clubs copy what wins two ways: an existing manager drifts a little inside its fingerprint, as far as its tactical flexibility allows and weighed against the club's identity, and new managers arrive carrying the current trend more fully.

The players' combined trait ambition and loyalty splits into two traits for everyone, loyalty to the club and ambition for a bigger stage, so players carry thirteen traits; staff add loyalty to a manager and ambition for the top job as their own.
items.accepted-risk: One more trait for every player, and the design documents' trait list changes again.

items.text: Each staff member carries a list of regions and leagues with a level for each, like the languages list: it starts from where the person was born and has worked, and grows by working there.

A player leaks the plan two ways: the controversy trait with low mood or a grudge against the manager sets a player's chance to leak, and an unhappy player also leaks through his agent to the press, set by the agent's own traits.
How a compact summary of each manager's fingerprint is kept for every season, since full match detail is kept only while recent and the AI reads the fingerprint over seasons.
Whether rewind and replays re-run the engine or store positions, given that a replay must survive an engine or protocol update and that stored positions cost save size.
items.resolution: Answered in session 8 by the technical robustness brief: saves carry a version and migrate forward, old engines are kept, and replays store frames plus seed and version.

items.text: How bonds and knowledge of players are stored for staff, since the relationship pairs are defined for players and staff change costs injuries through empty bonds.
How coaching licence requirements enter each competition's dated rule pack.
A squad holds only a few tactics well, a limit set by tactical coaching, and a player's grasp of a tactic the team stops using fades, as routine familiarity already does.
The engine emulator is also fitted on season runs, so it screens the 32 staff attributes, and only the attributes it flags run their full season-long check in the release run.
items.accepted-risk: The emulator needs season-run training data, which adds its own fitting runs before it can screen.

items.text: The engine today has no traits, personality, morale, familiarity, relationships, or cohesion. Aggression is the only personality-like value: it raises the foul and yellow-card chance. Players differ in decisions only through role and plan offsets, and decision noise falls as decisions and composure rise.
The word trait means two things on the board: a habit of play such as shooting from distance, and one of the thirteen personality traits. The brief's traits are habits; its personality is the traits.

The word trait means a habit of play, such as shooting from distance, as in the brief and the genre; the thirteen personality values are called personality attributes. Every earlier use of trait for a personality value now reads personality attribute.
All eleven criteria of the traits, personality, and chemistry brief are in scope, and the gaps are walked in the brief's order.

Each trait is sized so that its behaviour happens at a set multiple of the rate of similar players without it, for example about 1.5 to 2 times; the multiple is a design target per trait, and the check compares players with and without the trait in the same role and quality.
A player may carry any number of traits; every habit a player has is a trait, but no player carries two opposite traits, such as shoots from distance and never shoots from distance.
items.accepted-risk: A player with many traits stands out less, because stacked traits blur.

items.text: The game offers the genre list of about fifty traits, as Football Manager has, such as shoots from distance, dives into tackles, and plays one-twos.
items.accepted-risk: Many genre traits have no real rate to compare against, so their targets are design values measured against the game's own players.

items.text: A trait has no cost beyond the choices it changes: it costs exactly the worse options it sometimes picks, which the true-cause log shows.
The check for personality and cards bands how card rates spread across players against real data, so hot-heads and calm players appear in real proportion.
The whole spread of card rates from calm to hot-headed players matches the real spread between players of one position, and the league card total stays in its band.

An in-match setback, such as a goal against, going behind, or an own error, dips the confidence of the player at fault most and of the rest a little, each sized by pressure handling and determination, and the dip fades over minutes. Amended in session 8: this dip is the dip half of the momentum rule, and good events lift in the same way.
items.accepted-risk: One more short-lived state per player during a match.

items.text: The setback effect is checked by the existing bands on real game-state data: how teams play and score when behind must still hold.
A leader on the pitch makes defensive calls land, shortens nearby teammates' setback dips, and relays the manager's shouts so new instructions spread faster through the team.
Leadership is checked by the sensitivity test: changing the captain's leadership may move only defensive organisation, setback recovery, and how fast shouts spread.

Professionalism acts three ways: how fast a player grows in training; how well he looks after himself (recovery between matches, sharpness kept, and fewer knocks hidden); and off-pitch conduct (fewer fines and incidents, and a steadier dressing-room presence).

Professionalism is checked two ways: the career bands (peak age, decline, youth conversion) must hold with professionalism explaining part of the spread, and a season sensitivity check changes one player's professionalism and lets only his growth, condition, and conduct move.
Training together builds on-pitch understanding between two players only up to a middle level; the top level needs minutes together in matches.
Chemistry with the tactical system is checked against a design target for how many weeks a squad needs to learn a new tactic, measured on season runs.

The caps of the mind and familiarity families are sized by the five-match test: whatever the mood, personality effects, and chemistry, a top player still looks clearly better than an average player in the same role in about two of three runs of five matches.

The player reads mood, personality, and chemistry effects two ways: each player shows one short state line, such as settled, low after the error, or new to the system, with its effect in words; and the assistant names the biggest of these effects before and after the match.

A squad change stays fair two ways: losing all understanding and tactic grasp costs at most a small share of what a real quality gap costs, so a better new player helps at once; and understanding and grasp rise fastest at the start, so most of the loss returns within a few weeks.
Squad-change fairness is checked by a rotation band: teams that rotate a lot must not do worse than real data shows for heavy rotation.
Real match data can measure how much heavy rotation costs a team, so the rotation band has a real target.
Traits, personality attributes, and chemistry are the core of the area equally, and all three go into the first version.

The top risk of the area is stacked effects: mood, personality attributes, traits, and chemistry together could swamp ability even when each cap holds alone. The five-match test must run with every family switched on at once, not one family at a time. Answered in part by the soft combine, the team layer's own cap, and the tail band.

Coherence, session 8: older decisions that say twelve hidden personality traits now read thirteen personality attributes, after the split of ambition and loyalty and the naming decision that trait means a habit of play.

The design documents give traits a 1-to-100 scale and a list of twelve; the board now stores personality attributes on the 1-to-20 scale, thirteen of them, and traits as a separate list of about fifty habits. The documents change at the next reshape.

The four families of effective ability (body, mind, familiarity, surroundings) combine softly: each further effect in the same direction counts for less than the one before, so stacked effects fade out without a hard edge. This amends the rule that the family caps add.
items.accepted-risk: A soft combine is harder to explain and to tune than a plain sum.

items.text: Partnerships and cohesion keep their own separate cap in the team layer; only the four families share the soft combine.
The worst case of stacked effects is checked by a tail band: season runs count how often a top player has a run of very poor matches, and the rate is banded against real data.
Stacked effects show without the internals: the state line and the assistant speak in words about how the player is, and the game shows no sizes, no list of effects, and no net number.
Real data can give how often top players have a run of very poor matches: counted from public rating-site data, used only inside calibration.

In the engine today, the score changes behaviour only through the AI manager: from minute 70 a trailing team's mentality rises one step and pressing goes high, and from minute 80 a leading team's mentality drops one step with time-wasting. Players themselves do not read the score, and nothing models momentum or match importance.

Momentum comes from the mind family: good events (a goal, a big save, a near miss) lift confidence as setbacks dip it, sized by the same personality attributes, and both fade within minutes; a home crowd adds to the lift after a good home event.
items.accepted-risk: A second short-lived state per player, and a crowd term that must stay inside the measured home advantage.

items.text: Momentum is checked by a next-goal band: after a goal, how often the same team scores the next goal within a set time is banded against real data, so momentum can never make matches feel decided.

Real event data gives how often the scoring team also scores the next goal within a set time, with team strength removed. Partly: no paper publishes the rate, so the band must be computed from event data, and the best evidence puts the true effect near zero.

Match importance has three parts: the stakes (a final, a knockout tie, a title, relegation, or promotion decider, rising late in the season); rivalry (derbies, the crowd, and the audience); and what the match means to one player, such as facing a former club or a first start.
items.accepted-risk: A per-player importance value for every match adds work before each kick-off.

items.text: Pressure acts by pressure handling: a player with low pressure handling gets wider error tails, slower decisions, and a lean to safer options (the short pass over the shot) in important matches; a player with high pressure handling is lifted a little, a big-match player.

Pressure is checked by a big-match band: how finals, derbies, and deciders differ from ordinary matches in goals, cards, and errors is banded against real data. Amended in session 8: the band covers only fewer goals in finals and home advantage in derbies and cups; cards and errors stay unbanded.
Real data shows a measurable difference between big matches and ordinary ones. Partly: goals in finals and home advantage in derbies and cups are measured; cards and errors are not.

Players read the score and the clock themselves, not only through the manager: how much each player reacts is set by personality attributes, for example determination pushes a player harder when behind.

A comeback comes from four mechanisms, with no script: the trailing team takes more risk; the leading team's focus drops a little, more for players with low concentration or professionalism; substitutes bring fresh legs and a new shape; and a goal back lifts the trailing team and dips the leading one.
The reaction to the score is not fixed: the mentality the manager sets matters, some teams keep pressing when ahead to kill the match, and the reaction fades rather than lasting all match.
Comebacks are checked by a comeback band: how often a team that trails by one or two goals draws or wins, by the minute it fell behind, is banded against real data.
Which further comeback mechanisms does the person want beyond the four, and the set mentality, the kill-the-match choice, and the fade? The person said 'and more'.

Four more comeback mechanisms join: a red card changes the balance and the side with more players pushes; a home crowd pushes a trailing home team in added time, and late goals cluster in added time as real data shows; a leading team with low pressure handling tightens up late in an important match; and a trailing team sends its keeper up for a late set piece, more often in cups and on the final days of a league.
The manager's set mentality is the base of a player's reaction to the score, and each player's personality only leans a little within it; a player never overrides the mentality on his own.
The acceptance check bands possession and shot shares by score margin (behind by two, by one, level, ahead by one, by two), by 15-minute period, and by match importance, with team strength removed.
items.accepted-risk: Three-way cuts leave thin cells, so the band needs large batches and real data split the same way.

items.text: Momentum, pressure, game state, and comebacks are the core of the area equally, and all four go into the first version.

The area has three top risks: double counting, because players, the manager's mentality, momentum, and pressure all push the same way when behind, so the game-state effect could come out too large; thin data, because the next-goal, big-match, and three-way shares bands need finely split real data; and a stacked mind family, because momentum and pressure add two more mind effects under the soft combine, so the tail band may fail.

Coherence, session 8: momentum and pressure are mind-family effects, so they fall under the soft combine and the tail band; the setback dip is now the dip half of the momentum rule; and the crowd's part of the lift must fit inside the measured home advantage.

Coherence, session 8: pressure handling and composure keep the existing split. Composure acts on each action under a presser; pressure handling acts on the occasion, meaning how important the match is. The pressure rule reads pressure handling only.

The engine's rules today: offside is judged when a team-mate plays the ball and called when an offside player is the next to touch it, with level onside and no offside from throw-ins, goal kicks, or corners; the referee can play advantage and hold the card; a second caution sends a player off. The card comes from one draw raised by the tackler's aggression, not from how bad the foul was, and the referee has no strictness value. Extra time and shoot-outs run from the rule pack, with one fixed substitution pack.

The engine's offside has no edge cases: no interfering with an opponent without touching the ball (blocking the keeper's view), no reset when a defender deliberately plays the ball, no rebound off the keeper or post counted as the same phase, and no handling of a defender who has left the pitch.

The card follows the foul: each foul is graded careless, reckless, or excessive force from the tackle's speed, angle, and timing, and the referee's strictness moves the line between grades; context cards also apply, for denying an obvious goal-scoring chance, stopping a promising attack, and persistent fouling.

The engine implements the complete IFAB Laws of the Game, with each league's and competition's own differences, including every offside edge case: interfering with an opponent without touching the ball, a defender's deliberate play resetting offside while a deflection or save does not, a rebound off the post, bar, or keeper staying the same phase, and a defender off the pitch without permission still counting.
items.accepted-risk: The complete Laws are a large rule surface, and every clause needs its own scenario.

items.text: Tackling style is set two ways: a team instruction (stay on feet, normal, get stuck in) and a per-player instruction to tackle harder or ease off; players lean within them by aggression.
Cards and fouls are checked by a referee spread band: how card and foul rates spread across real referees in one league is banded, and the tackling setting must move the rates in the real direction.
Public data gives card and foul rates per referee over whole seasons, enough to band the spread between referees in one league.

The Laws are checked three ways: one set-up scenario per clause of each Law, and a Law counts as done only when all its clause scenarios pass; bands on real rates of offsides, penalties, and free kicks per match; and a review of sampled calls, where replays of random offside and foul calls are checked against the Law.
items.accepted-risk: The sampled-call review needs a person or a rule oracle to judge each replay.

items.text: The video referee is checked three ways against real data: an overturn band per match split into goals, penalties, and red cards; a band on how long reviews take and how much time they add; and a band on the clear errors it still misses.
Published reviews, such as a league's panel of key match incidents, give how many clear errors the video referee still misses per season, so that band has a real target.
Each competition breaks ties with its real order, for example goal difference first in England, head-to-head first in Spain and Italy, and UEFA's own rules for groups and knockout ties.

Each competition has its own full rule pack: substitutes and windows, bench size, concussion substitutes, extra time, shoot-outs, the video referee, tie-breakers, and registration. This replaces the one fixed pack the engine uses today.
The Laws, the referee, the video referee, and competition formats are the core of the area equally, and all four go into the first version. The person named no top risk.

Coherence, session 8: the referee's foul tolerance and card threshold now mean where the lines between careless, reckless, and excessive force fall; the team instructions gain a tackling setting beside line height, pressing, width, tempo, directness, and mentality; and the per-competition rule pack replaces the one fixed pack the engine has today.

Referees differ by about 1.5 times in yellow cards once teams are removed: across 7,203 top-five-league matches (2018-19 to 2021-22), the strictest referee showed 1.23 times the league rate and the most lenient 0.81 times (Royal Statistical Society journal, 'Yellow fever'). Per-referee fouls exist only as raw figures on statistics sites, with no team adjustment.

The Premier League's key match incidents panel counted 17 missed video-referee interventions in 2023-24 and 9 in 2024-25 over 380 matches each, about 0.02 to 0.045 a match, beside about 30 on-field errors a season.

Real evidence for momentum is weak: the same team scores the next goal more often than the opponent across 3,433 matches, but with no strength adjustment; a strength-adjusted survival study found a goal changes the timing of the next goal the same way for the team that scored and the team that conceded; no effect follows a goal just before half-time; and teams two goals up concede more soon after. No paper gives a next-goal rate with strength removed.
The momentum rule lifts a team after a good event, but the best strength-adjusted evidence finds momentum small or absent, so the next-goal band may force the lift to almost nothing.
items.resolution: The band decides the size; the state stays readable in words.

items.text: Big matches differ only partly: English cup finals average about 20 percent fewer goals than league matches (a press source, not strength-adjusted); Bundesliga derbies from 1999 to 2009 differ from other matches only in that home advantage disappears; and home advantage in cup matches is about half that in league matches (0.27 against 0.51 goals). No measured effect of derbies on cards was found.

No public study counts runs of very poor matches for top players; the tail band needs its own count from player-rating data, which sites such as WhoScored, SofaScore, and FotMob publish but do not license.

Rotation costs a little and less for rich squads: across 16,720 matches in four leagues (2010-11 to 2021-22), more rotation lowered points in England and France with negligible effect in Italy and Spain, and the cost shrank as squad value rose; a Chinese study found each step of rotation cut win chance by 6.4 percent in congested weeks; Bundesliga coaches who kept winning line-ups won no more often.
Momentum keeps its lift and dip, and the next-goal band decides their size: if the data puts momentum near zero, the effect on scoring is near zero, but the state is still shown in words.
The poor-run rate for the tail band is counted from player ratings on public rating sites, used only inside calibration; the data is not repackaged, shown, or sold.
items.accepted-risk: The rating sites' terms of use may not allow collection, the same accepted licence risk as the other calibration data.

items.text: The big-match band covers only what is measured: fewer goals in finals, home advantage lost in derbies and halved in cups. Cards and errors in big matches stay unbanded.

The attribute file today has nine goalkeeping attributes: handling, reflexes, aerial reach, one-on-ones, kicking, throwing, command of area, communication, and rushing out. Positioning is the shared outfield attribute, distribution is split into kicking and throwing, and sweeping is rushing out.
The nine keeper attributes stay: positioning is the shared attribute, distribution is kicking and throwing, and sweeping is rushing out, shown under those names on the keeper's profile.

A keeper's style comes three ways: the manager's keeper role (line keeper or sweeper keeper) sets the base, traits such as comes off the line, rushes out, or eccentricity lean the choices, and attributes decide how well the keeper does it.

Keeper distribution follows two instructions: the team's build-up instruction (play out short, mixed, go long) sets the base, and a keeper instruction chooses the targets (centre-backs, full-backs, the target man, fast throws); the keeper picks within them by pressure and his kicking and throwing.

Keepers are checked by four bands: the league save rate at about 65 to 75 percent; goals prevented (expected goals on target minus goals conceded) per keeper against the real spread; how often a save gives a rebound shot, by keeper handling; and sweeper actions outside the box per match, by keeper.
Public data gives goals prevented, rebound shots after saves, and sweeper actions per keeper per season, enough to band the spread between keepers.

Keeper effects are amplified like other players', so a top keeper stands out within a few matches; the goals-prevented band records a departure from the real spread on purpose, while the league save rate stays at 65 to 75 percent and the league goal bands hold.
items.accepted-risk: The goals-prevented band departs from real data on purpose.

items.text: Shot-stopping, style, and distribution are the core of the area equally, and all go into the first version. The person named no top risk.

Coherence, session 8: keeper amplification follows the rule that amplification stays at player level, so the league save rate, goals, and scoreline bands must still pass; keeper eccentricity is now one of the keeper traits; and the keeper instruction joins the in-match tools beside the team build-up instruction.
The engine today has no weather, no pitch quality, and no crowd: every match plays in the same conditions, and home advantage exists only if the realism test measures it from play.

Rain and wind act through the ball physics: rain lowers ball friction so the ball skids faster and raises the slip chance, and wind pushes the ball in flight, most on long and high balls; a cap keeps each condition's effect on goals and passing small.
items.accepted-risk: The caps are design values, because no public source measures rain or wind.

items.text: Pitch quality acts three ways: a poor pitch makes the ball bounce and roll less truly, which widens touch and pass errors, more for players with low technique; the pitch wears through the season by use and weather, which the groundsman slows; and a club can prepare its pitch (long grass, watered, narrow within the Laws) to suit its tactic.

Home advantage scales with the crowd: attendance and how full the stadium is set the home effect, from the measured empty-stadium level to the normal full level; the away support share lowers it; and travel distance lowers the away team's condition only very slightly. Jet lag across time zones stays as the travel decision sets it.
Weather stays small by condition bands: each condition (dry, wet, windy, worn) keeps its own band, and a limit caps how far apart the dry band and each other band may be.
Weather and pitch are the core of the area; the crowd and travel support them, and the effect of travel distance is very small. All of it goes into the first version.

The area has two top risks: the rain, wind, and pitch caps are design values with no real source, so their size is a guess; and the crowd, the referee's leaning, nervous players, late belief, and travel all add to home advantage, so the total could pass the home-advantage band.

Coherence, session 8: every part of home advantage (crowd on the referee, nerves, late belief, travel) shares the one measured home-advantage band, as the crowd assumption already requires; the band per condition gains a windy band and a limit on distance from the dry band.
Advanced analytical models are their own separate work group, an attempt to improve emergent play; the rest of the realism work does not wait on it.

The board's option score already follows the real choice model, which weighs completion, a running receiver, and a forward option far above threat; a player who chased threat alone would choose less like real players, so a threat model must earn its place in the comparison test.
The work group builds two versions: expected threat as the 'value gained' term inside the existing option score, and a full possession-value score; the comparison test picks the winner.
items.accepted-risk: Two models to build and fit, one of which is thrown away.

items.text: Pitch control feeds each player's picture of the pitch, limited by what that player scanned, so a player can misjudge space; passes, runs, and defending read space only through that picture.
The full models run in the watched match, and a cheap stand-in runs in background matches, with a check that results match.

The comparison test plays the same matches with each version and simpler rules, and compares three things: progression against real data (progressive passes and carries, entries to the final third and the box, possession chains); how often each version picks the option a real player picked in the same situation, from event data with freeze frames; and whether it stays inside the performance budget. The winner must be closer to real on the first two and inside the budget.

A cheap stand-in for background matches pulls against two earlier decisions: no realism lever is pulled, so background matches keep the full engine; and a result never depends on whether the match was watched.
items.resolution: Within this work group only, the full models run in the watched match and a cheap stand-in everywhere else; this is an accepted exception to the no-lever rule, and the risk that a result depends on watching is accepted.

items.text: Within the analytical-models work group, the full models run in the watched match and a cheap stand-in runs everywhere else. This is an exception to keeping the full engine in background matches.
items.accepted-risk: A result may depend on whether the match was watched.

items.text: The analytical-models work group comes last in the order of work, after all the other realism work, as a later improvement. Amended in session 8: only the in-play models and ghosting stay last; the display and staff models come early.

The work group has three top risks: real players weigh completion above threat, so both models may choose less like real players and leave nothing to merge; pitch control and possession value for 22 players may cost too much for the budget; and the choice-match test needs freeze-frame event data, which is thin in public data.

Coherence, session 8: the no-lever rule and the rule that a result never depends on watching now carry one named exception, the analytical-models stand-in; the fast model's equality check is unchanged.

Four more models join players' choices in the work group: a pass-completion model (the chance a pass reaches its target from positions, pressure, and pass type, the chance half of the option score); an off-ball scoring-opportunity model (pitch control times the chance the ball arrives times the scoring chance from there, which drives runs); receiver prediction (which team-mate the carrier will likely pick, so defenders anticipate and intercept); and a turnover and pressing model (the chance a press wins the ball here and now, which decides when to press).

Four models serve AI managers and staff: defensive ghosting (a learned model of where a typical defender stands, a positioning benchmark and a 'where he should have been' view); in-match win probability (AI substitutions and risk, staff advice, highlight swings); an Elo-style team strength rating (board expectations, AI, odds, and the fast model); and style and role detection from events (analysts, scouting, and player similarity).

Two models serve the analysis the player sees: action value (VAEP or on-ball value, crediting every action including defending, as the base of player ratings); and decision quality, which compares each choice with the best option in the player's own picture and shows missed options, possible only because the simulation knows the truth.
Each model starts fitted on real event and tracking data, then is refitted on the engine's own matches after each engine change; the comparison test watches for drift away from real.

Only models that change what happens in a match pass the comparison test and the budget: the in-play models, ghosting when defenders use it, and win probability for AI managers. Display models (action value, decision quality, style and role, and the team rating on screen) pass the one-record check only.

The display and staff models (team rating, win probability, style and role detection, action value, decision quality) come early, in the work that needs them; the in-play models and ghosting stay in the last work group.
Enough public tracking data exists to fit the in-play models and ghosting: about 74 full-tracking matches, with PFF used under the accepted licence risk.

Public full tracking of all 22 players and the ball adds up to about 74 matches: PFF's 64 matches of the 2022 World Cup at about 30 frames a second with synchronised events (free by request, terms not published), the DFL IDSSE set of 7 Bundesliga matches at 25 frames a second (CC-BY 4.0), and 3 Metrica sample matches (no formal licence). SkillCorner adds 10 A-League matches of broadcast tracking with partial visibility and pressing and run labels (MIT). StatsBomb 360 has 292 matches of event freeze frames, not continuous tracking, under a non-commercial agreement. Other sets (Last Row, Alfheim, SoccerNet, SoccerTrack) do not fit these models.

The published models used about as much data as is public: Spearman's off-ball scoring model used 58 matches of one league, Fernández and Bornn's space value used 20 matches, and Le and others' deep defensive ghosting used 45 matches, about 1.3 million frames.

Public data is enough for pitch control (few parameters, fits on IDSSE and Metrica), pass completion and receiver prediction (about 15,000 passes on clean licences, over 60,000 with PFF), pressing (SkillCorner labels plus IDSSE), and the pitch-control half of the off-ball model. Deep defensive ghosting needs PFF; the 7 clean IDSSE matches support only a simple regression ghost.

The PFF World Cup 2022 tracking set is used under the same accepted licence risk as StatsBomb and Transfermarkt: only derived statistics and fitted models reach the game, and no data is shipped. The models fit on PFF, IDSSE, SkillCorner, and Metrica together.
items.accepted-risk: PFF's terms are not published and may forbid commercial use.

items.text: Defensive ghosting aims for the deep imitation model from the start, fitted on the 64 PFF matches.
items.accepted-risk: One tournament of national teams may not describe club defending, and deep models cost more to run.

items.text: The engine today already runs a fixed-timestep loop whose match starts from a stored seed, and the same seed and build replay byte-identical on one machine.

A replay stores its recorded frames and also its seed and engine version, so it plays back without the engine after any update and can be re-simulated on the old engine for debugging; saves carry a version number and migrate forward with one migration per change.
items.accepted-risk: Stored frames make replays larger, and old engine versions must stay available for debugging.

items.text: Developers get three tools: a debug mode that records every random draw with its stream, the option scores, and the rule that fired, so any moment traces back to its causes; a bisect tool that re-runs a seed on two engine versions and finds the first tick where they differ; and an in-game bug report that attaches the save, the seed, and the version so a player's bug replays at once.

Retired and inactive people move to compact archive records, and old match detail compacts to summaries, as the history window already does for events, so the active database stays small over decades.

The benchmark requires that one matchday of every active league finishes within the player's matchday wait on the reference laptop and that a full season of every league fits the season-advance limit; a release check scans the build and fails if it contains licensed data.
