Three checks guard compatibility and growth: every release loads a stored save from each past version, migrates it, and plays a season; every release plays stored replays from each past version and re-simulates their seeds on the old engine to match the frames; and the 50-season check fails if season speed or save size after 50 seasons grows past a set margin over season one.
All parts of technical robustness are the core equally, and all of it goes into the first version. The person named no top risk.

Coherence, session 8: the gap on how saves and engine versions are numbered is now answered by versioned saves with one migration per change; old engine versions stay available, which the mid-match save rule and the replay re-simulation both need; and the licensed-data scan backs the rule that the game ships none of the calibration data.

The engine today splits its parts into files (fatigue, fouls, offside, steering, decisions, the AI manager), many written as pure functions that take players and a draw and return a result; one central step in the simulation owns the match, though steering still moves players in place. It has a three-hook plugin boundary (decision, rule, commentary), feature flags in the tuning file that switch a candidate model for a paired run, tuning values and rule packs in configuration, and a scenario module for constructed situations. It has no module interface or registry, no way to switch a module off by configuration, a modifier step only for fatigue, and one random stream in the code, although split streams are decided.

Every part of the engine is a module behind a typed interface, registered by name. A module reads a read-only view of the match state and returns results and proposed changes; only the central loop applies them. Each optional module has an off version, so its effect can be measured alone, and any module can be replaced by another that meets the same interface.
items.accepted-risk: Proposed changes and a read-only view add a copy or an apply step on every tick, which presses on the performance budget.

items.text: Each factor that changes an ability (fatigue, pressure, weather, momentum, and so on) is a modifier module that names its family; each family (body, mind, familiarity, surroundings) combines its modifiers, and the families combine softly. A new factor is added as a new modifier.

The quick engine stays a statistical model fitted from full-engine results, but it emits the same event types as the full engine, so every consumer (statistics, commentary, ratings, reports) reads both. It shares no calculation modules with the full engine, a deliberate departure from the brief.

A configuration file names the module and version used for each slot; each module carries a card (purpose, inputs, outputs, tuning values, and the calibration source and band) that a check requires to be complete.

The module contract is checked three ways: the interface gives a module only a read-only view, so the compiler refuses a module that writes the state; an off-switch run switches each optional module and each modifier off in turn, and the match must still finish and emit valid events; and a swap test puts a stand-in module in each slot, and the rest of the engine must run unchanged.
One refactor moves the engine to the module contract before the realism work starts, so every later work piece builds on it. It runs in stages, starting after the match-engine branch is handed off.
items.accepted-risk: The realism work waits for the refactor.

items.text: The area's top risk is effects that cross module lines: real football couples fatigue, pressure, and decisions tightly, so strict modules may hide or double an effect that spans two modules.

Coherence, session 8: the module refactor becomes a new first piece of work before the realism test harness; the soft combine of the four families is now the combining step of the modifier modules; the split random streams become one stream per module as well as per player and kind of action; and the quick engine's shared event types join the fast model's equality check.

The engine is about 16,200 lines. Match logic sits in impl blocks across nine files that write the simulation directly: about 35 writes in the referee rules, 17 in the ball and possession code, 9 in decisions, plus fatigue, the AI manager, tactic changes, snapshots, steering, and discipline. Fouls, offside, shot maths, fatigue maths, steering maths, and the AI's pre-match setup are already pure functions and move easily; the referee rules, possession, blocks and saves, and decisions (whose scoring draws noise inside itself) are tangled.

The engine has one random stream (ChaCha8) shared by 31 draw sites in decisions, rules, the simulation, and fatigue, so adding or moving one draw shifts every later draw. Splitting it into a stream per module changes every match outcome at once: it breaks the 12 test files that script referee or injury draws, breaks snapshot resume, and moves every realism band, so calibration must be redone.

The nearest seams today: three plugin hooks that adjust option scores, cards, and commentary but do not replace a part; a feature-flag framework whose code-flag list is empty and never read; tuning and rule packs as pure configuration; and a scenario builder that writes simulation fields directly, so it must be rewritten when the state moves. One hidden setting reads an environment variable during a tick (PARRY_BEHIND at sim.rs:1112), which a module contract would remove.

The match-engine workflow is at the review of its lone-forward slice (after the tuning loop), with its earlier architecture review passed with no blocker; the branch has not yet been handed off as a pull request.

The module refactor stays one piece of work before the realism work, done in stages: first split the random stream into one stream per module and per player and kind of action, recalibrate, and freeze a new baseline; then move the parts to the contract one at a time, each move holding that baseline exactly (same seeds, same events); the pure parts (fouls, offside, shot, fatigue, and steering maths, the AI's setup) move first, and the referee rules and possession last. Hidden settings, such as the environment variable read during a tick, are removed in the refactor.
The match-engine workflow finishes its review and hands off its branch as it is; the module refactor starts afterwards as its own workflow on the merged engine.

Forty screens sketch the whole game with every decision built, on the Broadcast Blue look: start, the week, players, staff, tactics, match day, training and medical, the market and youth, competitions and international duty, the club, and the career. Each screen lists the decisions it shows.
The sketch uses a dark broadcast look, while the product rules ask for a light scene first and no dark theme for the panels in the first release.
items.resolution: Keep dark: Broadcast Blue is the main look, and the product rules change to match it.

items.text: The game uses the dark Broadcast Blue look as its main look; the product rules that ask for a light scene first and no dark panels change to match it.

The sketch goes deeper in three groups: match day (extra time, penalties, red cards, the other manager's changes), players and staff (all 32 manager attributes, every staff role, a full player profile), and the season and world (international duty with jet lag and injuries, transfer windows, the job market over years).
The decided staff list has 25 roles, plus the manager. The number 33 in the staff room is the count of people in post, not the count of roles.

The decisions do not list the goalkeeper attributes. The sketch draws nine (aerial reach, command of area, communication, handling, kicking, one on ones, reflexes, rushing out, throwing) as a proposal; which set the game uses is open.

The harness holds sixteen bands in one content file, and each band passes when a point estimate falls inside a fixed range; the harness computes a standard error for every band but uses it only to label a change as noise, never to decide a pass.

The flag comparison already plays both arms on the same seeds, but it compares the two arms' totals separately with a fixed margin of 0.05, so it throws away the noise cancellation that paired seeds give.
Each match draws every random number from one ChaCha8 stream, so one added or removed draw shifts every later draw in the match.

A full-engine match costs about 448 ms on one core (about 2.3 matches a second); on the 8-core reference machine the harness plays about 12.6 matches a second, a full 1,000-match run of every suite takes about 81 minutes, and a targeted run of one pairing takes about 87 seconds.

Recent tuning swept 181 settings of the contest levers by hand at 200 matches each, and no setting passed every band; a tempo setting that fixed passes, throw-ins, and ball-in-play time broke the discipline bands and the stronger-team check, so it was held back.
Thirteen slow tests carry their own realism limits on 200 fixed seeds, separate from the bands file, so two sources of truth can drift apart.
The code has no optimiser, no emulator, and no sensitivity tool; every candidate setting costs a full engine run read by a person.
The harness keeps each match's event log only for outliers and bands only team and match totals, so no band reads a player, a position, or a sequence of play.

At today's 12.6 matches a second on 8 cores, the 1.5 million matches of a full release run take about 33 hours; an overnight run of 12 hours needs about 35 matches a second, and the realism work will make each match slower.
items.evidence: arithmetic from engine-speed-measured and the check load of session 7

items.text: At 1,000 matches the standard error of mean goals is about 0.053 goals, so a quick run cannot see a change smaller than about 0.1 goals (about 4 percent), and the goalless share of 6.3 percent is known only to about plus or minus 1.5 points.

To detect a 5 percent change in goals per match with 90 percent power needs about 3,300 matches per arm without pairing; with paired seeds at a correlation of 0.6 to 0.8 it needs about 700 to 1,300 pairs, but the correlation on this engine is not measured.

Failing to find a difference is not evidence of sameness; an equivalence test passes only when the whole confidence interval sits inside a margin set in advance, for example a fraction of how much real leagues differ from each other.

Hundreds of bands each tested at 5 percent raise false alarms on almost every run; the standard answer is a strict family rule (Holm) for a few gate bands and a false-discovery rule (Benjamini-Hochberg) for the rest, which are shown to a person, not used to block.

The Stockfish chess project judges every engine change on its test farm with a sequential test on paired games from the same opening, stated in fixed effect bounds and scored per pair, and stops each test as soon as the answer is clear.
Confidence sequences and e-values give a verdict that stays valid however often a developer looks at a running batch, which fits a run that stops early.

Paired seeds cancel noise only while both engines consume the same draws for the same events; one extra draw desynchronises everything after it, which is why each player and each kind of action needs its own stream.

History matching scores each output by its distance from the real value divided by the combined uncertainty of the emulator, the simulator's own noise, the data, and a model-discrepancy allowance, and rules a setting out when any score passes about 3; an HIV model cut its plausible space by a factor of about 10 to the 11th over six waves.

Mozilla's performance tracking, with a simple test per run across thousands of series, raised about 12.5 percent false alerts and missed about 6.8 percent of real regressions, so long-run tracking needs change-point methods and a person to triage.

Independent Poisson goals predict too few draws, about 10 percent fewer than observed; the Dixon-Coles correction with rho about -0.13 moves weight to 0-0 and 1-1, and a bivariate Poisson with a shared term does the same.
The scoring rate rises through a match and depends on the score, as Dixon and Robinson's 1998 model of goal times shows, so a flat rate per match is not real.
After a red card to the away team, the home team's scoring odds rise by about 69 percent and the away team's fall by about 42 percent.

A 2025 study puts skill at about 40 percent and luck at about 60 percent of how far clubs over- or under-perform in a season, against an older estimate of about 26 percent randomness, so the table's spread has a measurable luck share.

A hierarchical model of attack and defence per team (Baio and Blangiardo 2010), fitted on real results, gives a predicted spread for any statistic, so the engine can be compared with that spread instead of a range set by hand; such checks are conservative and miss small errors at the league level.
Copula models join shots for and shots against, and newer work joins shots, touches, and a hidden tactical state, which is the published form of a joint band.

The Waymo self-driving challenge scores a simulator by how likely the real recorded movement is under the simulated distribution, feature by feature in three groups (movement, contact with others, and staying on the road), summed into one realism score.
A classifier trained to tell real play from simulated play scores realism by its accuracy, with 50 percent as the target, but it can learn artefacts of the data instead of behaviour.
Blind real-or-simulated tests use about 4 to 10 raters on tens of short clips with an agreement score; raters near 50 percent correct mean the two are indistinguishable.
Nash averaging over a round-robin of strategies rates each strategy against the whole field and ignores copies, while a plain win rate or Elo hides rock-paper-scissors cycles.
Football Manager's public history shows corner and narrow-formation exploits and unreal crossing while season figures look plausible: averages can be right while play is wrong.
Out of the Park Baseball checks itself by simulating thousands of seasons from real opening-day rosters and comparing the results with what happened.

Tracking and event data give distributions to compare: pass-network shape, team convex hull (about twice as large in attack as in defence), team length and width, pressing intensity, possession chain length, and speed and acceleration.

Morris screening finds which of p settings matter in about r times (p + 1) runs, for example about 510 runs for 50 settings, while Sobol indices cost about 100 times as much and are best kept for the few settings that survive.

A Gaussian-process emulator weakens beyond a few tens of inputs, needs at least about 10 design points per input, and a heteroscedastic form predicts the spread as well as the mean; a Sobol design can grow in later waves.
Chess engines tune hundreds of values at once: SPSA moves every value together along a random direction and reads the result of two short matches, and Texel tuning fits values to results by gradient.
With many bands, the practical loss for one optimiser is the worst band's distance in units of its tolerance; true multi-objective search weakens past a few objectives.
Changing one setting at a time cannot see two settings that act together and can stop at a false best; factorial and space-filling designs find main effects and interactions from the same runs.
Multi-fidelity methods spend most runs on a cheap model early and the expensive one late; here the ladder is the fast model, then shortened matches, then the full engine.

The rule that every band is an output and never a tuning target pulls against the emulator's first role, a tuning tool that proposes settings toward the bands; once the emulator is trusted, the engine's confirmation can become a formality.
The design documents state bands as fixed real ranges, while the board decided that tolerance is the real spread widened by sampling noise; the two rules disagree where one statistic appears in both.
The release run of about 1.5 million matches pulls against an engine that plays about 12.6 matches a second on 8 cores today, about 33 hours, before the realism work slows each match.
Split the bands into a few dozen gate bands, judged under a strict family rule, that can block a change, and watch bands, judged under a false-discovery rule, that go to a person's dashboard.

Fit a hierarchical model of real football (goals, shots, cards, timing, the table) on the five seasons of data, and compare the engine with its predicted spread for each statistic instead of ranges set by hand.
Judge each change as the chess test farm does: paired seeds per match, a sequential test with fixed bounds per gate band, and a stop as soon as the verdict is clear.
Use today's flag comparison to measure how strongly paired matches correlate before and after the stream split, because the whole per-change budget depends on that number.
Give every band one implausibility score that combines sampling noise, data error, and a design allowance, and fail a run when any gate band scores above 3.

Write the sensitivity family as a library of stated relations (raise finishing, goals must not fall; unrelated bands stay equivalent), each checked with a sweep across several levels instead of one before-and-after pair.

Score the engine against tracking data as the Waymo challenge does: speeds, accelerations, distances to others, pressing distance, and line heights, each as a likelihood, summed into one realism score tracked per version.
Turn the watched review into a blind test: short real and simulated clips in the same 2D view, several raters, and a pass when raters cannot tell them apart.
Rate the round-robin of styles with Nash averaging, and flag a style whose rating against the field is far above its plain win rate.

Four feedback tiers: seconds (smoke matches and determinism), minutes (emulator prediction and a small paired batch), about an hour (a gate run with a sequential test), and overnight (every band, every family).
Store each baseline run under a hash of engine version, content, and seeds, so an unchanged baseline is never played twice.
Run an optimiser (CMA-ES or SPSA) against the emulator, where a trial costs milliseconds, then confirm its best proposals on the full engine.
Keep a set of bands that no tuning run may read, and judge every tuned setting on them, as a model is judged on data it never saw.
Keep every band in one registry that the slow tests, the harness, and each module's card read by name, so a threshold lives in one place.
Store every run and show each band over versions with change-point detection, so slow drift that no single change shows is caught.
The realism test must answer all four failures: bands that fight each other under hand tuning, a slow verdict, noise that the pass rule cannot see, and play that looks wrong while the averages pass.
items.why: The person named all four as true today.

items.text: A developer learns within about five minutes whether a change made realism better or worse on the bands it touches.
items.why: A coffee-length wait keeps the loop fast enough to tune by, and about 3,800 matches fit at today speed.
items.accepted-risk: The budget holds about 3,800 matches at today speed; if the realism work halves the engine speed, it holds about 1,900, and the per-change check must shrink or stop earlier.

items.text: The talk goes into the statistical model and the pass rule first, as the foundation for the change check, tuning, and the checks beyond averages.
Of the four failures, invisible noise can wait longest: the first version of the new harness may keep today fixed ranges while the other failures are answered.
items.accepted-risk: Every other tool reads the pass rule, so until the noise fix lands the change check and the tuning can chase noise, and a band can drift inside its fixed range unseen.

items.text: The yardstick is split: a statistical model fitted on the five real seasons judges goals, scorelines, results, and the table, and measured ranges judge passes, fouls, cards, running, and the other statistics.
items.why: The published models are strong for results, and weaker for the other counts.
items.accepted-risk: Two kinds of band to build and explain, and an error in the fitted model becomes an error in the test.

items.text: The yardstick compares whole-league totals, not results per gap in team strength.
items.accepted-risk: The comparison is fair only when the generated leagues have the same strength spread as the real ones; an engine where favourites win too often can pass on totals.

items.text: Comparing league totals only pulls against the three-layer league bands and the fast-model check per pairing of team strengths, which both compare by strength, and against a fitted results model, which predicts by team strength. Resolved: the yardstick compares per strength gap after all.

The yardstick compares results and goals for each gap in team strength, so real and generated teams both carry a strength rating; this fits the three-layer league bands, the fast-model check per pairing, and the fitted results model.
items.why: League totals are fair only when the generated leagues copy the real strength spread.
items.accepted-risk: A strength rating is needed for every real team in the five seasons and for every generated team.

items.text: A band passes by an equivalence test: the whole confidence interval of the engine statistic must sit inside the band margin, so a small or noisy run cannot pass by luck and may return not sure yet.
Every band can block a change; there are no watch-only bands.
items.accepted-risk: Under a strict family rule each band needs about 2.4 times the matches of a single test at 300 bands, so the five-minute budget cannot hold every band in one change run.

items.text: Every change run judges every band, and the wait for a verdict grows to about an hour.
items.accepted-risk: Nothing slips past a change, but the loop is slow, and an hour holds about 45,000 matches at today speed.

items.text: Each band margin is a fixed share of how much real leagues and seasons differ on that statistic, for example half, set in advance and never after a run.
When a band comes back not sure yet, the developer sees the interval and the margin and decides whether the change goes ahead.
items.accepted-risk: The call depends on judgement under time pressure, and a hurried yes can let a bad change sit until the overnight run.

items.text: Which share of the real spread sets each margin (a half, a third, or a quarter), and how the share applies to design targets.

Judging every band on every change takes about an hour, which pulls against the five-minute verdict budget decided earlier in the session. Resolved: both hold, and a harness performance project makes every band fit in about five minutes.

Both budgets hold: a verdict on every band within about five minutes, which makes the harness fast enough through more cores, a lighter measuring build, and cached baselines, a performance project of its own.
items.accepted-risk: This needs about 12 times today throughput before the realism work slows each match, and until that project lands neither budget is met.

work.summary: The test-only output written from one match record, bands with a real target and a design target, the conversion of StatsBomb bands to the DFL schema, and the watched review that replays a real match beside a simulated one. It goes first because every later mechanism is reviewed against it.
work.stale-because: Session 7 changed the harness: bands per league, tier, and group with tolerances widened by noise; every scoreline and the full table; stored reports per version; the sensitivity family, the round-robin, the fit check, and the exploit hunt; the fast-model equality check; the error and turnover bands; and the check cadence: about 1,000 matches per change, split random streams, early stopping, touched parts per milestone, and an overnight release run. Later in session 7: behaviour, crowding, crowded-pass, and frozen-player bands, a recompute test for every figure, and the explanation playtest. Also: the forked-match change check with paired seeds over every in-match tool. Also: set-piece goal share, per-routine, penalty, shoot-out, and team set-piece spread bands. Also: running by 15-minute period and season injury bands on counts, burden, types, recurrence, and congestion. Also: a multi-season check of ten fifty-season saves banding title turnover, fortune churn, and up and down rates, plus a streak band. Session 8 added movement bands against tracking data and a check band for match preparation. Session 8 adds turn-rate and acceleration bands.

work.title: Write the team shape and the block design document (step 2 of 12)
work.entry: /wf task write the Team shape and the block design document (W-02, Engine realism programme, step 2 of 12 in the realism sequence), grounded in .ai/workflows/brainstorm-realism-additions-20260922/01-brainstorm.md and every findings document its card lists
work.summary: The block law (the team slides with the ball at a measured gain), the width in each phase, and the nine phases derived from the engine state. It is the first mechanism, and the first watched review judges it.

criteria.text: Traits adjust decision weights, for example a player who tries long shots chooses shooting from distance more often.
Personality affects card risk.
Personality affects reaction to setbacks.
Personality affects leadership.
Personality affects professionalism.
Chemistry develops through familiarity between teammates, built up through training and matches.
Chemistry develops through familiarity with the tactical system, built up through training and matches.
Effects are modest and understandable: players see their impact without these factors overpowering ability.
Traits that are purely cosmetic.
Chemistry systems so strong that squad changes feel punished.
Players with a trait show the associated behaviour at a measurably higher rate than those without it.
Momentum after key events is small in effect and fades within minutes.
Pressure scales with match importance and affects players according to their composure and big-match temperament.
Game state changes behaviour: teams leading typically cede possession and defend deeper, while teams behind take more risks.
Comebacks happen occasionally through realistic mechanisms, not scripting.
Excessive momentum that makes matches feel predetermined.
Teams behaving the same regardless of the score.
Possession and shot shares for leading and trailing teams follow real-world patterns across a batch of matches.
The Laws of the Game are implemented, including offside with correct timing, advantage, foul severity leading to appropriate cards, and second-yellow dismissals.
Referee profiles vary in strictness and consistency.
VAR is available by competition, with reviews for goals, penalties, and red cards.
Competition formats support extra time, penalty shootouts, varying substitution rules, squad registration limits, and tie-breakers.
Missing offside checks in edge cases.
Card rates that do not respond to referee strictness or tackling style.
Card and foul rates vary appropriately with referee profile and team aggression settings.
Separate attributes for positioning, reflexes, handling, command of area, one-on-ones, distribution, and sweeping.
Handling affects rebounds, which create second chances.
Distribution style links to the team's build-up tactics.
Save percentages broadly in the region of 65 to 75 percent across a league.
Goalkeepers being too dominant or too weak.
No distinction between shot-stopping and sweeping styles.
Save percentage and goals conceded against xG vary sensibly with goalkeeper quality.
Weather has modest effects: rain speeds up the ball and increases slips; wind affects long passes; heat increases fatigue.
Pitch quality affects technical play.
Home advantage is calibrated to real data and adjusts with crowd size.
Weather effects too strong and random-feeling.
Home advantage much larger than in reality.
Home and away win rates match target ranges, and weather effects are measurable but small.
Pitch control models help players assess space when making passes and runs.
Expected Threat (xT) or Expected Possession Value (EPV) helps the AI judge whether a pass or carry improves the attack.
These models can be displayed to the player in post-match analysis.
Computation is efficient enough for real-time use or approximated where needed.
Models too computationally expensive for background matches.
Models used for display but not reflected in behaviour.
AI decisions guided by xT or EPV produce more realistic progression patterns than simpler rules, confirmed through comparison testing.
Determinism: fixed time steps and stored seeds allow exact replays.
Performance: background matches run quickly enough to simulate many leagues without slowing the game.
Exploit testing: automated searches for tactics or player combinations that break realism.
Data sourcing: a clear decision on real versus fictional players, with licensing considered.
Versioning so saved games and replays remain compatible after updates.
Logging and debugging tools to trace unexpected results.
Non-reproducible bugs.
Slow simulation as the database grows.
Exploits found by players after release.
Performance benchmarks are met for a full season of background fixtures, and replays reproduce exactly.

briefs.name: Match engine, game architecture, plugins, and composability

criteria.text: The match engine is made up of separate modules, each responsible for one part of the simulation.
Modules communicate only through defined interfaces, not by calling each other's internals.
Any module can be replaced with another version that meets the same interface, without changes elsewhere.
Every optional module has an off version so its effect can be measured in isolation.
A single shared match state holds all match data; only the central match loop changes it.
Modules return results and proposed changes rather than editing the match state directly.
Player abilities used in calculations pass through a sequence of modifiers (such as fatigue, pressure, weather), and new factors are added as new modifiers.
The engine's output is a stream of match events; statistics, commentary, ratings, and replays are built from that stream separately.
Which modules are used, and their tuning values, are set in configuration rather than in code.
The same seed, inputs, and configuration always produce the same match.
Each module uses its own random number stream, so replacing one module does not change the others' results.
The quick engine and the full engine share the same core calculation modules and produce the same types of events.
Every module can be tested on its own, using constructed match situations.
Every change is checked against realistic match statistics over a large number of simulated matches.
Two versions of a module can be run side by side on identical matches and their results compared.
Each module documents its purpose, inputs, outputs, tuning values, and the real-world figures it was calibrated against.
